sections.title: Geotextiles
sections.summary: Geotextile strength (grab, puncture, tear) is for survivability; wovens (< 50% elongation) need more strength than nonwovens (> 50%). AOS keeps soil from passing, permittivity sets flow; UV stability needed; durability 'well in excess of 1000 yrs' (as printed); use polypropylene, not polyester, at pH > 9.
sections.body: Strength matters most: the geotextile must survive truck traffic over the aggregate even with some rutting, and on wet soil it must drain to avoid a waterbed effect without letting soft soil squeeze through. Strength for survivability is measured by grab, puncture and tear strength (Section 3.3.2). Elongation at break is typically less than 50% for wovens and greater than 50% for nonwovens; materials that elongate more survive better, so strength requirements are greater for wovens. AOS, essentially the largest opening, keeps larger soil particles from passing; flow capacity is measured by permittivity. UV stability is required and the geotextile should be covered soon after placement. Durability depends on polymer (polypropylene or polyester) and additives; as printed, durability life 'should be well in excess of 1000 yrs'. Polyester is a concern at high pH (pH > 9, e.g., with lime or cement stabilization), where polypropylene should be used. (p. 9-48)
key_points: Strength set by grab, puncture and tear for survivability (p. 9-48).
Wovens < 50% elongation need more strength than nonwovens (p. 9-48).
Use polypropylene, not polyester, at pH > 9 (p. 9-48).

sections.title: Geogrids
sections.summary: Geogrids are extruded, woven (coated) or welded; strength (wide width, junction) is for survivability; apertures must interlock with the gravel, neither too small nor too large; less UV-prone than geotextiles but still cover promptly; use polypropylene or polyethylene at pH > 9.
sections.body: Geogrids are characterized by manufacture (extruded, woven or welded; woven grids are usually coated), polymer and openings. Strength for survivability is measured by wide width and junction strength (Section 3.3.2). Apertures, measured directly, must suit the gravel above for interlock (lateral restraint): too small and gravel slides over, too large and interlock and confinement are lost. Geogrids are less susceptible to UV than geotextiles of the same polymer but should still be covered soon. Durability depends on polymer (polyethylene, polypropylene or polyester) and additives; at pH > 9 polypropylene or polyethylene geogrids should be used. (p. 9-49)
key_points: Apertures must suit the gravel for interlock (p. 9-49).
Polypropylene or polyethylene at pH > 9 (p. 9-49).
sections.applicability: Selecting geotextile, geogrid or geocomposite properties for stabilization.

sections.title: Geocomposites
sections.summary: Stabilization geocomposites (woven/nonwoven, geotextile/geogrid, nonwoven with high modulus filaments, geotextile/geonet) need component bonding sufficient for installation and service, plus drainage properties (Section 8); sliding between components reduces performance.
sections.body: Geocomposites for stabilization include woven/nonwoven geotextile composites, geotextile/geogrid composites, nonwoven geotextiles with high strength/modulus inline filaments, and geotextile/geonet composites. Besides the component survivability, opening and durability requirements, the bond between components must keep their integrity in installation and service, and drainage composites need the compressibility and hydraulic properties of Section 8. Sliding of one geosynthetic over another reduces performance in stabilization (Christopher and Schwartz 2010). (p. 9-49)
key_points: Component bonding must hold through installation and service (p. 9-49).
Sliding between components reduces performance (p. 9-49).

sections.title: Design Overview
sections.summary: Design overview for geosynthetic separation and stabilization: design-by-function with AASHTO M 288, the FHWA (2008) steps, and the Caltrans selection flow chart.
sections.body: This section covers design considerations (3.3.1), design steps for separation and stabilization (3.3.2) and primary design references (3.3.3) (p. 9-50).
sections.applicability: Designing geosynthetic separation and stabilization layers.

sections.title: Design Considerations
sections.summary: Design considerations for separation and stabilization geosynthetics: filtration compatibility, survivability and endurance, design by function with AASHTO M 288, the Caltrans (2014) selection chart, and a composite support equivalent to CBR = 3 (MR 4500 psi).
sections.body: A separator geotextile must prevent intermixing of the permeable base and the subgrade or subbase, satisfy filtration criteria for the subgrade gradation and permeability, and satisfy survivability and endurance criteria (FHWA 2008) (p. 9-50). For stabilization the geosynthetic must also separate, filter wet, often saturated subgrades and reinforce, with stronger survivability criteria; design is by function with AASHTO M 288 following FHWA (2008). The structural pavement design is not modified, but the subgrade support value can be improved. Caltrans (2014) developed the flow chart in Figure 9-5 for selection based on subgrade strength and gradation and the gradation compatibility of the base/subbase (p. 9-52). The pavement is designed as if the geosynthetic were absent; the geosynthetic replaces extra unbound material for construction and no part of the pavement section. If the soil has CBR less than 3 and the aggregate thickness is set by a low rutting criterion, the composite system is theoretically equivalent to CBR = 3 (resilient modulus 4500 psi), to be confirmed by plate load or FWD testing. The FHWA procedure is controlled by soil CBR measured per ASTM D4429.
key_points: Pavement is designed as if the geosynthetic were not present (p. 9-52).
With CBR < 3 subgrade and a low rut design, the composite support is theoretically equivalent to CBR = 3 (MR 4500 psi).

sections.title: Design Steps
sections.summary: Design steps from FHWA (2008) for geosynthetic separation (CBR >= 3) and stabilization (CBR < 3) applications. Subsections cover: Separation; Stabilization.
sections.body: Design steps are given for separation (3.3.2.1) and stabilization (3.3.2.2) applications, after FHWA (2008) (pp. 9-52 to 9-60).
sections.applicability: Following the FHWA design procedures for geosynthetics in roadways.

sections.title: Separation
sections.summary: FHWA (2008) separation design: need for a separator (CBR about 3 to 8, high fines), opening and permittivity per Table 9-6, retention and permeability checks (Eqs. 9-6 to 9-8), Class 2 survivability, and at least 6 in. of base between wheel and geotextile.
sections.body: Step 1: assess need; separators suit high fines subgrades (CL, CH, ML, MH, CM, GM, OL, OH) with CBR about 3 to 8 (MR about 4500 to 12,000 psi, Su about 2000 to 5000 psf, R about 18 to 37) (p. 9-52). Step 2: maximum opening and minimum permittivity from AASHTO M 288 (Table 9-6, p. 9-53): Class 2 grab strength 250 lb (1100 N) for elongation < 50% and 157 lb (700 N) for > 50%; sewn seam 220 (990) and 140 (630); tear 90 (400) and 56 (250); puncture (D6241) 495 (2200) and 309 (1375); UV 50% retained after 500 hours; AOS < 0.6 mm for < 50% passing No. 200 and < 0.3 mm for > 50%; permittivity > 0.02 sec-1 and > that of soil. Values are minimum average roll values in the weaker direction; acceptance per ASTM D4759 and D4354 (p. 9-54). Check AOS, permeability and permittivity with Eqs. 9-6 to 9-8; for noncohesive silts and highly pumping soils use AOS <= D85 and lab filtration tests. Step 3: survivability; use Class 2 for subgrade CBR > 3 with at least 6 inches of base/subbase and normal equipment and for edgedrain filters; Class 1 (Table 9-7) for CBR < 3 and heavy equipment; keep at least 6 inches of base/subbase between wheel and geotextile. Very poor subgrades (R <= 5, CBR about <= 1.5) may warrant stronger than Class 1 (Caltrans 2014) (p. 9-56). Step 4: follow Section 3.2.1.
key_points: Separation applies to high fines subgrades with CBR about 3 to 8 (p. 9-52).
Table 9-6 Class 2: grab 250 lb (< 50% elongation) or 157 lb (> 50%); AOS < 0.6 mm or < 0.3 mm by fines; permittivity > 0.02 sec-1 (p. 9-53).
Keep at least 6 in. of base/subbase between the wheel and the geotextile at all times (p. 9-54).
For noncohesive silts use AOS <= D85 and run laboratory filtration tests.

sections.title: Stabilization
sections.summary: FHWA (2008) stabilization design: design pavement without the geosynthetic, take 50% of extra mixing aggregate t1, construction platform thickness t2 from Figure 9-6 with Nc 5, 5.5, 6 (geotextiles) or 5.8 (geogrid with separator), filtration (Eqs. 9-6 to 9-8) and survivability per Tables 9-7 and 9-8.
sections.body: Steps (FHWA 2008) (p. 9-56): (1) identify subgrade CBR, groundwater, AASHTO/USCS class and sensitivity; (2) compare with Section 3.1.3.1 or local policy to decide if a geosynthetic is needed; (3) design the pavement without the geosynthetic; (4) determine any extra aggregate t1 to ameliorate mixing at the base/subgrade interface and reduce it by 50%; (5) determine the aggregate t2 for a construction platform from Figure 9-6 (the same charts as Section 2.3.2.1), selecting for geotextiles Nc = 5 for low ruts (< 2 in.), 5.5 moderate (2 to 4 in.), 6 large (> 4 in.), and for geogrids with a geotextile separator Nc = 5.8 for low to moderate rutting; Giroud and Han (2004a, 2004b) may also be used for geogrids (p. 9-58); (6) select the greater of t2 or 50% t1; (7) check filtration (Eqs. 9-6 to 9-8), or for geogrids the aggregate per Section 2.3 or a geotextile with the grid; (8) survivability: geotextiles per AASHTO M 288 class (Table 9-7, p. 9-55: Class 1 grab 315 lb (1400 N) / 200 lb (900 N), seam 280 / 180 lb, tear 110 / 80 lb, puncture 620 / 433 lb, AOS < 0.43 mm or < 0.3 mm, permittivity 0.5, 0.2 or 0.1 sec-1 for < 15, 15 to 50, > 50% passing No. 200; woven slit film not allowed) and geogrids per Table 9-8 (p. 9-60: multi-rib tensile 1230 lb/ft (18 kN/m) Class 1, 820 (12) Classes 2 and 3; junction strength 25 lb (110 N) for Classes 1 and 2 and 8 lb (35 N) for Class 3; aperture 0.5 to 3 in. with D50 <= aperture <= 2 D85 of aggregate; separation D15 aggregate < 5 D85 subgrade). Default is Class 1 for stabilization; very poor subgrades (R <= 5, CBR about <= 1.5) may need stronger than Class 1 (p. 9-59).

Nc for geotextiles: 5 (< 2 in. ruts), 5.5 (2 to 4 in.), 6 (> 4 in.); geogrid with separator: 5.8 (p. 9-58).
Select the greater of t2 or 50% of t1.

sections.title: Geosynthetics Overview of Construction Specifications and Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Specifications, quality assurance and monitoring for geosynthetic stabilization layers. Subsections cover: Specification Development; Summary of Quality Assurance; Summary of Instrumentation Monitoring and Construction Control.
sections.body: This section covers specification development (3.4.1), quality assurance (3.4.2) and instrumentation monitoring and construction control (3.4.3) for geosynthetic stabilization layers (p. 9-61).
sections.applicability: Specifying and checking geosynthetic stabilization.

sections.title: Specification Development
sections.summary: Specifications for geosynthetic stabilization layers from AASHTO M 288, AASHTO R 50-09 and FHWA-NHI-07-092 and GeoTechTools: survivability, retention and filtration requirements, seams, sequencing and an engineer's representative on site.
sections.body: Detailed specifications are in AASHTO M 288 (2014a), AASHTO R 50-09 (2014b), FHWA-NHI-07-092 (FHWA 2008) and GeoTechTools; each gives guide specifications to be modified for local conditions and example specifications (p. 9-61). Main considerations are minimum geosynthetic requirements from survivability, retention and filtration (Section 3.3) and construction requirements (Sections 3.2 and 3.3), including seam lap and sewing, construction sequencing and quality control. An engineer's representative should be on site to confirm the correct geosynthetic, the specified sequence and that no damage occurs.
sections.applicability: Writing geosynthetic stabilization specifications.

sections.title: Summary of Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Quality assurance for geosynthetic stabilization: subgrade condition, aggregate placement, lift thickness, equipment, GPS and DCP checks, rut limits, proofrolling, and exhuming about 1 ft2 to inspect for damage.
sections.body: Attention should be paid to factors affecting survivability: subgrade condition, aggregate placement, lift thickness, equipment operations and visual observations (p. 9-62). Primary quality control is moisture, density or stiffness and thickness of aggregate above the geosynthetic; GPS with point checks; DCP for strength and effective depth. Rutting should be limited to tolerable design levels; fill ruts and do not blade them down. Proofroll. After the initial lift, excavate a small section to expose approximately 1 ft2 or more for damage; if damaged, examine more sections, repair by replacement or patch, and increase initial lift thickness and/or use lighter ground pressure equipment.
key_points: Expose approximately 1 ft2 or more of geosynthetic after the first lift to inspect for damage (p. 9-62).
sections.applicability: Field quality checks on geosynthetic stabilization.

sections.title: Summary of Instrumentation Monitoring and Construction Control
sections.summary: Monitoring geosynthetic stabilization: rut depth, FWD or LFWD for an equivalent subgrade resilient modulus, instrumented proofrolling, intelligent compaction, and strain-gaged geosynthetics.
sections.body: Monitoring typically measures rut depth against the geosynthetic and gravel design (p. 9-62). If the stabilization layer is incorporated in the pavement design, FWD or LFWD tests can give an equivalent subgrade stiffness, a valid equivalent subgrade resilient modulus for design given that the geotextile mitigates long-term degradation from intrusion and pumping. Instrumented proofrolling and intelligent compaction confirm uniformity and composite stiffness. The geosynthetic can be instrumented with strain gages offsite to evaluate stress/strain at the subgrade; one product is sold with fiber optic strain gages built in.
sections.applicability: Verifying performance of geosynthetic stabilized subgrades.

sections.title: Geosynthetic Cost Data
sections.summary: Cost data for geosynthetic stabilization: geosynthetic stabilization costs: separation geotextiles about $1.00/yd2 in place, stabilization geotextiles $1 to $2.50/yd2, geogrids $1.50 to $4.00/yd2, gravel $7 to $20/ton, and typical aggregate thickness reduction of 20 to 40%.
sections.body: This section gives the cost components of geosynthetic stabilization (p. 9-63).
sections.applicability: Estimating the cost of geosynthetic stabilization.

sections.title: Cost Components
sections.summary: Geosynthetic stabilization costs: separation geotextiles about $1.00/yd2 in place, stabilization geotextiles $1 to $2.50/yd2, geogrids $1.50 to $4.00/yd2, gravel $7 to $20/ton, and typical aggregate thickness reduction of 20 to 40%.
sections.body: Cost components are the geosynthetic (by the square yard), placement and any additional stabilization aggregate (per ton) (p. 9-63). Equipment is common to highway projects; very soft subgrades may need light equipment, adding cost with or without geosynthetics. In-place cost of separation geotextiles is on the order of $1.00/yd2; for soft soil stabilization $1 to $2.50/yd2 for geotextiles and $1.50 to $4.00/yd2 for geogrids; in-place compacted gravel $7 to $20/ton. Compared with thicker aggregate alone, the geosynthetic typically reduces aggregate thickness by 20 to 40%. Assuming in-place gravel at 120 lb/ft3, a six-inch layer costs on the order of $1.80 to $5.40/yd2, a typical saving for a CBR = 2 subgrade, plus savings from not over-excavating and disposing 6 inches of subgrade and better long-term performance.
key_points: Separation geotextile in place about $1.00/yd2; stabilization geotextiles $1 to $2.50/yd2; geogrids $1.50 to $4.00/yd2 (p. 9-63).
Geosynthetics typically reduce aggregate thickness by 20 to 40%.
A 6 in. gravel layer at 120 lb/ft3 costs about $1.80 to $5.40/yd2.
sections.applicability: Comparing geosynthetic stabilization cost with thicker aggregate.

sections.title: Mechanical Stabilization: Lightweight Fill
sections.summary: Lightweight fill (geofoam, foamed concrete, wood fiber, tire shreds, expanded shale and clay, fly ash, boiler slag, air-cooled slag) as an alternative to aggregate replacement for pavement subgrade stabilization over deep soft deposits.
sections.body: An alternative to replacement with aggregate is lightweight fill, including geofoam, foamed concrete, wood fiber, tire shreds, expanded shale and clay, fly ash, boiler slag, air-cooled slag and others (p. 9-64). They should especially be considered in deeper deposits where shallow surface stabilization may not be effective and thicker aggregate would control deformation under wheel load but increase concerns for settlement and stability. The materials are covered in the Lightweight Fill chapter; this section focuses on their use for stabilization of pavements and refers to that chapter.
sections.applicability: Pavement subgrade stabilization over deep compressible soils where added weight is a concern.

sections.title: Feasibility Considerations
sections.summary: Feasibility of lightweight fill for pavement support: caution with degradable materials such as wood fiber, buoyancy and uplift of very light materials (down to 0.70 lb/ft3) under flooding, anchoring cover, and differential icing over insulating materials.
sections.body: Practically any lightweight fill in Chapter 3 is feasible for improving pavement support, but caution is advised for materials that could degrade over time (e.g., wood fibers), which could harm ride quality and structural integrity (p. 9-64). Materials range from the lower end of soil unit weights down to 0.70 lb/ft3; the lighter end raises concern for buoyancy and uplift of the pavement (Figure 9-7). The design must be checked for uplift where flooding or a rising water table can reach the layer, requiring an anchoring system (e.g., soil fill on top) or other measures (p. 9-65). Insulating materials (e.g., geofoam) raise differential icing concerns in cold regions. The primary issue is the pavement support the materials provide.
key_points: Lightweight fills down to 0.70 lb/ft3 raise buoyancy and uplift concerns (p. 9-64).
Check uplift where flooding or a rising water table can reach the layer; provide an anchoring soil cover (p. 9-65).
figures: Figure 9-7: Uplift due to flooding of pavement section using lightweight fill.
sections.applicability: Screening lightweight fill for pavement stabilization.

sections.title: Applications
sections.summary: Lightweight fill reduces settlement and increases stability for pavements over soft subgrades and deep compressible deposits, giving immediate improvement that can accelerate construction despite higher cost.
sections.body: Lightweight fill can reduce settlement and increase stability for pavements over soft subgrades and should especially be considered for deep compressible deposits (p. 9-65). Although more costly than most other stabilization methods, it gives immediate improvement and accelerates construction; on some projects the time saving may be worth more than the cost difference.
sections.applicability: Pavements over deep compressible soils needing fast construction.

sections.title: Advantages and Potential Disadvantages
sections.summary: Heading for the advantages (9.4.1.2.1) and potential disadvantages (9.4.1.2.2) of lightweight fill stabilization.
sections.body: Heading for the advantages and potential disadvantages of lightweight fill stabilization, 9.4.1.2.1 and 9.4.1.2.2; it has no text of its own. (p. 9-65)
sections.applicability: Weighing lightweight fill against other stabilization methods.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.summary: Lightweight fill speeds construction and eases access, reduces settlement and stability problems, suits many projects, may mitigate frost by insulation, and can give more uniform support, most important for pavements.
sections.body: Potential advantages: accelerated construction with fewer site access problems (larger loads with lighter equipment); reduced settlement and stability problems; suitability for a wide variety of projects; potential frost mitigation from thermal insulation; and potential for more uniform support, the most important for pavements. (p. 9-65)
key_points: Accelerates construction; reduces settlement and stability problems (p. 9-65).
More uniform support, most important for pavements (p. 9-65).
sections.applicability: Weighing lightweight fill against other stabilization methods.

sections.title: Potential Disadvantages
sections.summary: As in the Lightweight Fill chapter: fill may not be locally available; it is usually costlier than other methods except local recycled materials; some leach; some need protection such as encapsulation; thermal properties can cause differential icing.
sections.body: The disadvantages in the Lightweight Fill chapter apply equally: fill may not be locally or regionally available, affecting selection and cost; except for local recycled materials, lightweight fill stabilization is usually more expensive than other methods (p. 9-66); some fills may generate leachate; some need protection for durability (e.g., encapsulation); and geothermal properties could cause differential icing of the pavement. (pp. 9-65 to 9-66)
key_points: Usually costlier than other stabilization methods (p. 9-66).
Insulating fills can cause differential icing (p. 9-66).
sections.applicability: Weighing lightweight fill against other stabilization methods.

sections.title: Feasibility Evaluations
sections.summary: Heading for geotechnical, environmental and site feasibility of lightweight fill stabilization (9.4.1.3.1 to 9.4.1.3.3).
sections.body: Heading for the feasibility evaluations of lightweight fill stabilization, 9.4.1.3.1 to 9.4.1.3.3; it has no text of its own. (p. 9-66)
sections.applicability: Site screening for lightweight fill pavement stabilization.

sections.title: Geotechnical
sections.summary: Key: subgrade sensitivity, strength and soft deposit depth, plasticity (expansion, frost), and especially the water table, since some fills float or absorb water. Fills behave like granular soils (wood fiber, slags, fly ash, ESCS, tire shreds) or have unconfined strength like cohesive soils (geofoam, cellular concrete).
sections.body: As for other technologies, subgrade sensitivity and strength and the depth of soft deposits are key, with the subgrade's plasticity (expansive clays, frost heave). The groundwater table is especially critical, since some fills float and several absorb moisture and gain weight when saturated for long. The fill must be characterized: per the Lightweight Fill chapter, fills behave like granular soils (wood fiber, blast furnace slag, boiler slag, fly ash, expanded shale, clay and slate (ESCS), tire shreds) or have unconfined compressive strength and behave like cohesive soils in undrained loading (geofoam, cellular concrete). (p. 9-66)
key_points: Water table especially critical: some fills float or absorb water (p. 9-66).
Granular-like fills vs fills with unconfined strength (p. 9-66).
sections.applicability: Site screening for lightweight fill pavement stabilization.

sections.title: Environmental Considerations
sections.summary: The groundwater table governs buoyancy and leachate; some fills can contaminate groundwater, deplete oxygen or change pH (listed per material in the Lightweight Fill chapter); disposal of excavated material also matters.
sections.body: The groundwater table is a critical environmental consideration for buoyancy and leachate. Some fills can contaminate groundwater, deplete oxygen or change its pH; the Lightweight Fill chapter's design section lists these per material. Disposal of excavated material is also a consideration. (p. 9-66)
key_points: Groundwater governs buoyancy and leachate (p. 9-66).
sections.applicability: Site screening for lightweight fill pavement stabilization.

sections.title: Site Conditions
sections.summary: Key site items: clearing and grubbing, stratigraphy and subgrade type, strength, stiffness and sensitivity, water table depth, topography for drainage, large consolidation over deep soft deposits, and on-site disposal.
sections.body: The most important site characteristics are clearing and grubbing, stratigraphy including subgrade type, strength, stiffness and sensitivity, groundwater depth, and topography for subgrade drainage. For deep soft deposits, large consolidation settlement is also important; on-site disposal of excavated material is also a site consideration. (p. 9-67)
key_points: Large consolidation over deep soft deposits matters (p. 9-67).
sections.applicability: Site screening for lightweight fill pavement stabilization.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.summary: Limitations of lightweight fill stabilization: environmental concerns both ways, availability, cost and long-term performance of some materials, offset by the wide choice of materials.
sections.body: Limitations relate to environmental concerns (the fill's impact on the environment and the environment's effect on the fill), availability, cost and long-term performance of some materials (p. 9-67). With many materials to choose from, one will likely suit a given project.
sections.applicability: Recognizing limits on lightweight fill use.

sections.title: Construction and Materials
sections.summary: Construction and materials for lightweight fill stabilization, referring to the Lightweight Fill chapter: construction of lightweight fill: granular forms and chips placed in compacted layers, geofoam blocks or panels, foams or slurries in forms, compaction to maximize density without degradation, and volume reduction from compaction and loading.
sections.body: This section covers construction (4.2.1) and materials (4.2.2) for lightweight fill used in pavement stabilization (p. 9-67).
sections.applicability: Building lightweight fill stabilization layers.

sections.title: Construction
sections.summary: Construction of lightweight fill: granular forms and chips placed in compacted layers, geofoam blocks or panels, foams or slurries in forms, compaction to maximize density without degradation, and volume reduction from compaction and loading.
sections.body: The Lightweight Fill chapter summarizes construction of each material, including placing, compacting and protecting against durability threats (p. 9-67). Granular forms (slag, fly ash, expanded shale) and chips (wood, tire shreds) are placed in layers and compacted; geofoam is placed in blocks or panels; some materials are placed as foams or slurries in forms. Compaction equipment is chosen to maximize density while preventing degradation, and volume reduction from compaction and shrinkage under soil cover and pavement is accounted for.
sections.applicability: Placing lightweight fill beneath pavements.

sections.title: Materials
sections.summary: Lightweight fill materials used in highway construction, with their typical geotechnical design and construction parameters, composition and sources, are given in the Lightweight Fill chapter of the manual.
sections.body: An overview of common lightweight fill materials used in highway construction, with typical design and construction parameters and their composition and sources, is in the Lightweight Fill chapter earlier in the manual (p. 9-67).

sections.title: Design Overview
sections.summary: Design overview for lightweight fill under pavements: design considerations, resilient modulus values (Table 9-9), design steps and references. Subsections cover: Design Considerations; Design Steps; Primary Design References.
sections.body: This section covers design considerations (4.3.1), design steps (4.3.2) and primary design references (4.3.3) for lightweight fill stabilization (p. 9-68).
sections.applicability: Designing pavements over lightweight fill.

sections.title: Design Considerations
sections.summary: Pavement design over lightweight fill: conventional fill procedures plus durability and other checks, little effect with at least 3 ft of gravel cover, resilient modulus as the key value (Table 9-9), a minimum 24 in. pavement system, and transition settlement gradient not over 1:200.
sections.body: Conventional fill design procedures apply to granular lightweight fills, plus checks of durability, water absorption, corrosion, combustion, erosion and environmental impacts (p. 9-68); NYSDOT (2015) covers tire shred compression, separation and combustion-preventing geometry; geofoam under pavements is covered in NCHRP Report 529 (Stark et al. 2004a) and Web Document 65 (Stark et al. 2004b). With a minimum of 3 feet of good quality gravel cover between pavement and lightweight material, the material has little impact on pavement design, even tire and geofoam; with thinner cover its support value must be determined. Resilient modulus is the most important value; CBR and subgrade reaction correlations are even more questionable than for soils, so laboratory resilient modulus tests are better. Table 9-9 (p. 9-69): geofoam (EPS) 1-2 pcf, CBR 2 to 4, MR 725-1450 psi; foamed concrete 20-62 pcf, CBR 15 to 150, E28 days 44-450 ksi; wood fiber 45-60 pcf, CBR 1, 1500 psi; tire shreds 45-60 pcf, 1/100 sand; ESCS 50-65 pcf, similar to gravel; fly ash 70-90 pcf, CBR 1 to 15 (Class C increases with time); boiler slag 50-65 pcf and air-cooled slag 70-94 pcf, CBR > 250, similar to or better than gravel. Field resilient modulus tests on the cover soil are ideal. A minimum pavement system thickness of 24 inches should be used above most lightweight fills other than durable gravel type fills. The transition to embankment soil should be gradual, with a calculated settlement gradient not exceeding 1:200 (vertical:horizontal).
key_points: At least 3 ft of good quality gravel cover makes the lightweight fill of little impact on pavement design (p. 9-68).
Resilient modulus is the most important pavement design value; lab resilient modulus tests are preferred.
Use a minimum pavement system thickness of 24 in. above most lightweight fills (p. 9-69).
Transition settlement gradient should not exceed 1:200 (vertical:horizontal).
Table 9-9: geofoam CBR 2 to 4 and MR 725-1450 psi; boiler and air-cooled slag CBR > 250.

sections.applicability: Assigning pavement support values to lightweight fill and detailing the cover and transitions.

sections.title: Design Steps
sections.summary: Design steps for lightweight fill stabilization: Section 2.3.2 thickness methods with increased thickness for CBR < 80 or the Giroud and Han method, proofrolling, blending (e.g., sand with at least 30% sand for tire chips), and NCHRP 529 geofoam design catalogs with a 24 in., 130 pcf preliminary dead load.
sections.body: The design steps of Section 2.3.2 apply to granular lightweight fill, but Figures 9-1 and 9-6 were developed for aggregates with CBR > 80, so thickness must be increased for lightweight aggregate with CBR < 80 or estimated by an alternate method (e.g., Giroud and Han in FHWA 2008); proofrolling should confirm the thickness (pp. 9-69 to 9-70). Granular lightweight fill is often blended with poorer soils; the modulus of tire chips is very low, but a sand-tire chip mixture (as low as 30% sand, Edil 2006) restores the modulus to about that of sand; Section 2.3.2.2 blending methods apply. Resilient modulus is the primary parameter for the layer and the equivalent stabilized subgrade. Class C fly ash is cementitious and can be used as an admixture (Section 6). For geofoam, NCHRP Report 529 and Web Document 65 give flexible and rigid design procedures: a low volume road catalog gives the structural number by EPS type, reliability and traffic, then AASHTO (1993) or state manuals set layer coefficients, with minimum AC and base thicknesses by ESALs; rigid catalogs give slab thickness by EPS type, reliability, ESALs, modulus of rupture and edge support/load transfer. For preliminary dead load use 24 inches thickness and 130 pcf (NCHRP 529).
key_points: Figures 9-1 and 9-6 assume aggregate CBR > 80; increase thickness for lightweight aggregate with lower CBR (p. 9-69).
A sand-tire chip mixture with as little as 30% sand restores modulus to about that of sand (Edil 2006) (p. 9-70).
Preliminary pavement dead load over geofoam: 24 in. at 130 pcf (NCHRP 529).

sections.summary: Specifications for lightweight fill under pavements follow the Lightweight Fill chapter, modified to require specified resilient modulus and durability, with FWD or LFWD performance monitoring.
sections.body: Specifications, quality assurance and monitoring for lightweight fill are covered in the Lightweight Fill chapter (p. 9-71). Typical specifications should be modified to require that materials meet the specified resilient modulus and durability requirements for pavement support. Performance monitoring could include FWD or LFWD testing to confirm compliance and gather data for future design. Specifications are on the GeoTechTools website.

sections.summary: Cost data for lightweight fill used in pavement subgrade stabilization are those given in the Lightweight Fill chapter, which apply equally here, with more information on GeoTechTools.
sections.body: Cost data in the Lightweight Fill chapter apply equally to lightweight fill for pavement subgrade stabilization; more information is on GeoTechTools (p. 9-71).
