sections.title: Mechanical Stabilization: Recycled Materials
sections.summary: Recycled materials for subgrade stabilization: reuse of reclaimed asphalt pavement (RAP) and recycled concrete (RCP, RCM) as unbound aggregate, plus foundry sand; in-place recycling and slab fracturing used as base are excluded.
sections.body: Recycled materials for subgrade stabilization are of two forms: reuse of pavement materials themselves, and recycled waste materials as stabilizers or aggregate substitutes (p. 9-72). The first, the main use, is recycled concrete pavement (RCP) or reclaimed asphalt pavement (RAP) from the site or hauled in. The second involves mostly lightweight materials covered in Section 4; foundry sand and recycled concrete materials (RCM) from pavement and non-pavement projects are reviewed here. Of the asphalt recycling techniques (hot mix, hot in-place, cold mix, cold in-place, full depth reclamation), only removal and reuse of asphalt as unbound aggregate for subgrade stabilization is reviewed; in-place methods add foamed asphalt or emulsion and produce base or subbase. RAP is usually milled and pulverized. Concrete slab fracturing (crack and seat, break and seat, rubblization) produces in-place base and is not considered; poor subgrades often exclude these. RCP is crushed to sand and gravel sizes and is combined with other concrete as RCM. See FHWA-RD-97-148 (FHWA 1997a).
key_points: Only RAP and RCM used as unbound aggregate to stabilize subgrades, and foundry sand, are covered (p. 9-72).
Crack and seat, break and seat and rubblization produce base layers and are not considered for subgrade stabilization.
sections.applicability: Using recycled pavement materials and foundry sand as stabilization aggregate.

sections.title: Feasibility Considerations
sections.summary: Feasibility considerations for recycled materials in subgrade stabilization. Subsections cover: Applications; Advantages and Potential Disadvantages; Feasibility Evaluations; Limitations.
sections.body: This section covers applications, advantages and disadvantages, feasibility evaluations and limitations of recycled materials for subgrade stabilization (pp. 9-73 to 9-75).
sections.applicability: Screening recycled materials for stabilization.

sections.title: Applications
sections.summary: Recycled pavement materials, on site or hauled in, provide a stabilization layer beneath the pavement section, and RAP and RCM may also give an improved base over marginal subgrades.
sections.body: Pavement materials are recycled on site or hauled from another site to give a stabilization layer where subgrade improvement is needed (p. 9-73). RAP and RCM may also provide an improved base course over marginal subgrades; base/subbase applications are covered in FHWA (1997a).
sections.applicability: Recycled stabilization layers beneath pavements.

sections.title: Advantages and Potential Disadvantages
sections.summary: Heading for the advantages (9.5.1.2.1) and potential disadvantages (9.5.1.2.2) of recycled pavement materials.
sections.body: Heading for the advantages and potential disadvantages of recycled materials, 9.5.1.2.1 and 9.5.1.2.2; it has no text of its own. (p. 9-73)
sections.applicability: Weighing recycled aggregates for stabilization.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.summary: RAP or RCM cuts reconstruction and disposal cost and conserves aggregate; properly designed and built, pavements with recycled materials have performed as well as those with natural gravel.
sections.body: Using RAP or RCM can reduce pavement reconstruction cost and waste disposal cost and conserve the diminishing aggregate supply. Properly designed and constructed, pavements with recycled materials have performed as well as those with natural gravel. (p. 9-73)
key_points: Performs as well as natural gravel when properly designed and built (p. 9-73).
sections.applicability: Weighing recycled aggregates for stabilization.

sections.title: Potential Disadvantages
sections.summary: Recycled material is less uniform; RAP may carry contaminated base; 100% RAP has a much lower CBR than gravel; residual oil may need setbacks from watercourses; RCM can leach tufa that clogs drains, degrades in freeze-thaw, and being highly alkaline (and salty) corrodes aluminum or galvanized pipe.
sections.body: Disadvantages: less uniform than quarried aggregate, especially when commingled from several sources, though good quality control usually handles this for stabilization; RAP commingled with contaminated base/subbase from over grinding or excavation; 100% RAP has a much lower CBR than gravel; residual oil and contamination may cause environmental issues, and some agencies require a minimum separation from watercourses; crushed concrete may leach 'tufa' like precipitates (a white pasty substance from unhydrated cement) that clog adjacent drains; RCM is susceptible to some freeze/thaw degradation, so test durability within the frost zone; and its high alkalinity, plus chlorides from deicing salts, can corrode aluminum or galvanized steel pipes in moisture (p. 9-74). (pp. 9-73 to 9-74)
key_points: 100% RAP has a much lower CBR than gravel (p. 9-73).
RCM tufa can clog adjacent drains (p. 9-73).
RCM alkalinity corrodes aluminum or galvanized pipe (p. 9-74).
sections.applicability: Weighing recycled aggregates for stabilization.

sections.title: Feasibility Evaluations
sections.summary: Heading for geotechnical, environmental and site feasibility of recycled materials and in-place recycling (9.5.1.3.1.a, 9.5.1.3.1, 9.5.1.3.2; the print numbers the first two both 5.1.3.1).
sections.body: Heading for the feasibility evaluations of recycled materials, 9.5.1.3.1.a, 9.5.1.3.1 and 9.5.1.3.2 (the print numbers Geotechnical and Environmental Considerations both 5.1.3.1); it has no text of its own. (p. 9-74)
sections.applicability: Evaluating a site for recycled material or in-place recycling.

sections.title: Geotechnical
sections.summary: Recycled aggregate raises the same issues as thicker gravel or geosynthetics; find groundwater and nearby water bodies. For in-place recycling, subgrade type, base contamination and groundwater are key; the subgrade must carry grinding or rubblizing equipment, and wet sites should be drained first.
sections.body: Printed with the same number, 5.1.3.1, as the next heading (Environmental Considerations), as printed. The geotechnical issues of recycled aggregate for stabilization, as thicker gravel or with geosynthetics, are practically those of those sections; groundwater and nearby water bodies should be located for environmental reasons. For recycling a project's pavement, subgrade type, in-place base and subbase quality (contamination) and groundwater are key. The recycling method depends on subgrade strength, which must carry the grinding or rubblization equipment; where soils are wet or saturated, drains should be installed and the site dewatered before in-place recycling. (p. 9-74)
key_points: Subgrade must carry grinding or rubblizing equipment (p. 9-74).
Drain and dewater wet sites before in-place recycling (p. 9-74).
sections.applicability: Evaluating a site for recycled material or in-place recycling.

sections.title: Environmental Considerations
sections.summary: Recycling is weather sensitive: many processes use water, so cold matters, and rubblizing in wet weather can destabilize the subgrade through impact pore pressures; noise, vibration effects on nearby structures, dust, groundwater and runoff control must be considered.
sections.body: The primary environmental considerations are weather related: many processes use water, so cold is a concern, and exposing the subgrade to wet weather while rubblizing or cracking concrete can cause severe disturbance or instability from pore pressure under dynamic impact. Noise from vibration and impact, especially under urban noise restrictions, and effects on nearby buildings must be considered, and dust may be an issue. Groundwater location and runoff control matter according to the recycled material's contamination potential. (p. 9-74)
key_points: Rubblizing in wet weather can destabilize the subgrade (p. 9-74).
Consider noise and vibration on nearby structures (p. 9-74).
sections.applicability: Evaluating a site for recycled material or in-place recycling.

sections.title: Site Conditions
sections.summary: For pavement recycling (TRB 2006 E-C087): survey distress, evaluate the existing structure (layers, thicknesses, shoulders) and soils (type, CBR or Mr, moisture). For stabilization, site needs are as for thicker gravel; review the gravel section if blending.
sections.body: To judge the feasibility, type and method of pavement recycling, the key elements (TRB Transportation Research Circular E-C087, Rubblization of Portland Cement Concrete Pavements, TRB 2006) are: a distress survey (cracking, joint deficiencies, surface defects, miscellaneous distresses); evaluation of the existing structure (layer types and thicknesses, shoulder condition); and soil conditions (types, bearing value such as CBR or Mr, moisture) (p. 9-75). For subgrade stabilization, site requirements are like those for thicker gravel (clearing and grubbing, water table and drainage, subgrade type, strength, stiffness and sensitivity); geosynthetics control disturbance better; on-site disposal and large consolidation of deep soft deposits matter; if recycled materials are blended, review the thicker gravel section's site considerations. (pp. 9-74 to 9-75)
key_points: Distress survey, structure evaluation and soil conditions (TRB 2006) (p. 9-75).
Bearing value as CBR or Mr (p. 9-75).
sections.applicability: Evaluating a site for recycled material or in-place recycling.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.summary: Limitations of recycling for stabilization: the fractured section must carry multiple equipment passes, in-place recycling may not be feasible on very soft (CBR <= 2) or highly sensitive subgrades, and high water must be addressed first.
sections.body: During in-place recycling the fractured pavement section must support multiple equipment passes (p. 9-75). In-place recycling may not be feasible where subgrade soils are very soft (e.g., CBR <= 2 based on the experience of several DOTs) or highly sensitive. High water levels should be addressed before in-place recycling.
key_points: In-place recycling may not be feasible on subgrades with CBR <= 2 or highly sensitive soils (p. 9-75).
sections.applicability: Recognizing where in-place recycling will not work.

sections.title: Construction and Materials
sections.summary: Construction and material controls for recycled aggregate stabilization layers: construction of recycled stabilization layers follows thick granular layer practice: soft ground equipment, a limit of a few inches of rutting, and functioning underdrains installed well ahead of recycling.
sections.body: This section covers construction (5.2.1) and materials (5.2.2) for recycled stabilization layers (p. 9-76).
sections.applicability: Building recycled aggregate stabilization layers.

sections.title: Construction
sections.summary: Construction of recycled stabilization layers follows thick granular layer practice: soft ground equipment, a limit of a few inches of rutting, and functioning underdrains installed well ahead of recycling.
sections.body: Construction follows the thick granular layer practice: soft ground equipment (low ground pressure wide track dozers, extended backhoes and excavators, partially loaded dump trucks) to avoid disturbance; disturbance in sensitive soils can lead to significant overuse of gravel; equipment rutting the subgrade or granular layer more than a few inches should not operate (p. 9-76). Underdrains (installed or existing) should function, especially when recycling the existing pavement over weak subgrade or high water; install them as far in advance of recycling as possible; they also drain the section during rain.
sections.applicability: Placing recycled stabilization material and preparing drainage.

sections.title: Materials
sections.summary: Material controls for RAP and RCM: gradation and density, steel removed, no oversized uncrushed pieces, RAP in RCM limited to 20%, fines control, washing to reduce tufa and salts, stockpile testing, standard compaction and subgrade strength checks.
sections.body: Gradation and density must be controlled for all recycling methods (p. 9-76). Reinforcing steel must be removed before RCM is crushed and screened. Uncrushed oversized pieces should not be placed, as they hinder uniform compaction or create voids. For composite pavements, RAP content in RCM should be limited to 20 percent to prevent loss of bearing strength and stiffness (FHWA 1997a). Fines (smaller than No. 200) must be controlled for drainage; washing may remove fines, dust, impurities and road salts, and washing RCM reduces tufa; only RCM without significant unhydrated cement or free lime should be used. Each stockpile should be tested (gradation, moisture, density, leach). Natural aggregate compaction requirements apply, using vibratory rollers. Subgrade strengths must be checked before and after recycling, and fines from intrusion or contaminated base minimized (p. 9-77).
key_points: Limit RAP content in RCM to 20% (FHWA 1997a) (p. 9-76).
Use only RCM without significant unhydrated cement or free lime, to control tufa.
Check subgrade strength before and after recycling (p. 9-77).
sections.applicability: Specifying recycled aggregate quality for stabilization.

sections.title: Design Overview
sections.summary: Design of RAP and RCM stabilization layers as for natural aggregates: laboratory resilient modulus, durability and drainage, FWD field trials, and corrosion and environmental checks.
sections.body: Design requirements for RAP and RCM aggregates are essentially those of natural aggregates, evaluated against the property requirements of the material they replace (p. 9-77). Pavement support values (resilient modulus) should be determined from laboratory tests, with durability and drainage assessed; FWD field trials to confirm as-constructed properties are recommended. Durability is critical for many of these materials, and corrosion potential (especially RCM) and environmental impacts must be assessed.
key_points: Determine the pavement support value from laboratory tests and confirm with FWD field trials (p. 9-77).
sections.applicability: Designing stabilization layers of recycled aggregates.

sections.title: Design Considerations
sections.summary: Design depends on the improvement the recycled material gives: hauled-in RCM, RAP or foundry sand can be lab tested before placement and QC/QA targeted at those properties; recycling in place needs lab tests during crushing or field sampling, in situ tests or test pits, and a subgrade investigation to confirm rubblization is possible.
sections.body: Pavement design depends on the improvement the recycled material provides. Hauled-in RCM, RAP and foundry sand can be treated as aggregate, tested in the laboratory before placement for design properties, with construction QC/QA targeting those properties. For recycling existing pavements, design must rely on laboratory tests of material sent during crushing or on field sampling and testing; in situ tests after placement and/or test pits must be done, and a thorough subgrade investigation must show whether the pavement can be rubblized. (p. 9-77)
key_points: Hauled-in material: lab test before placement (p. 9-77).
In-place recycling: in situ tests or test pits after placement (p. 9-77).
sections.applicability: Assigning design properties to RAP, RCM and foundry sand stabilization layers.

sections.title: Recycled Asphalt
sections.summary: RAP can usually be screened only to a 2 in. maximum size; contaminated base removed with it spoils drainage; RAP CBR is typically 20 to 25% with about 10 times the plastic strain of natural aggregate (Edil 2011); blends with 40% RAP have exceeded CBR 150 after 1 week (FHWA 1997a).
sections.body: RAP can often only be screened down to a maximum size of 2 inches; if much contaminated, fines-rich base comes off with the asphalt, hydraulic properties may be poor. RAP's CBR is typically on the order of 20 to 25 percent, and permanent deformation is much greater than for natural aggregate, on the order of 10 times greater plastic strain (Edil 2011). Blending with natural aggregate strengthens it significantly over time; aggregates with 40% RAP have given CBR values exceeding 150 after 1 week (FHWA 1997a) (p. 9-78). (pp. 9-77 to 9-78)
key_points: RAP screened to about 2 in. maximum (p. 9-77).
RAP CBR typically 20 to 25%; about 10 times the plastic strain (p. 9-77).
40% RAP blends exceeded CBR 150 after 1 week (p. 9-78).
sections.applicability: Assigning design properties to RAP, RCM and foundry sand stabilization layers.

sections.title: Recycled Concrete
sections.summary: RCM is designed like conventional aggregate: highly angular, CBR 90 to more than 140%, comparable to crushed limestone; pH above 11 corrodes aluminum or galvanized pipe; drains through or beside it need open graded gravel filters with no geotextile across that interface because of tufa.
sections.body: Design requirements for RCM in embankments are the same as for conventional aggregates. RCM is highly angular, with CBR from 90 to more than 140 percent depending on the original aggregate's angularity and the cement matrix strength, comparable to crushed limestone. Its high alkalinity (pH greater than 11) can corrode aluminum or galvanized steel pipes in direct contact in moisture, a design concern for utilities, guard rail posts and the like. Edgedrains and deep drains through or beside the layer should allow for tufa: open graded gravel, designed as a filter for the RCM, is placed against the stabilization material with no geotextile across that interface, and geotextiles may be used beneath or above the layer and around the rest of the drain. (p. 9-78)
key_points: RCM CBR 90 to more than 140%, like crushed limestone (p. 9-78).
pH above 11 corrodes aluminum or galvanized pipe (p. 9-78).
No geotextile across the RCM-drain interface; gravel filter instead (p. 9-78).
sections.applicability: Assigning design properties to RAP, RCM and foundry sand stabilization layers.

sections.title: Waste Recycled Material
sections.summary: Other recycled materials (foundry sand, lightweight fill materials, glass and tire shreds for drainage) must meet the properties of what they replace. Foundry sand has CBR about 4 to 20 and Mr about 6,000 to 30,000 psi, good for subgrade stabilization (Edil 2006), with strict moisture control; above about 6% bentonite it is nearly impermeable.
sections.body: Other recycled materials can replace natural gravel for base stabilization (e.g., foundry sand and many lightweight fill materials) and sometimes drainage aggregate (e.g., glass, tire shreds); they must meet the same property requirements as the material replaced, with durability and environmental issues assessed. Foundry sand is the waste of clay-bonded (e.g., bentonite) or chemically bonded (e.g., phenolic urethane) sand used for casting molds and cores, with carbon additives such as coal dust (Edil 2006). It has CBR values of about 4 to 20 and Mr of about 6,000 to 30,000 psi, less than base gravel but generally equal or better than subbase, so it is a very good candidate for subgrade stabilization aggregate (Edil 2006). Bentonite, varying between foundries and within stockpiles, requires strict moisture control in compaction (p. 9-79); high bentonite (e.g., above 6%) may make it rather impermeable, usable as a partial encapsulation cover over moisture sensitive soils, checked by permeability tests. (pp. 9-78 to 9-79)
key_points: Must meet the properties of the material replaced (p. 9-78).
Foundry sand CBR about 4 to 20, Mr about 6,000 to 30,000 psi (p. 9-78).
Bentonite above about 6% makes it nearly impermeable (p. 9-79).
sections.applicability: Assigning design properties to RAP, RCM and foundry sand stabilization layers.

sections.title: Design Steps
sections.summary: Design steps for recycled stabilization: Section 2.3.2 for aggregate replacement, Section 3.3.2 with geotextiles, increased thickness for recycled material with CBR < 80 or the Giroud and Han method, proof rolling, and FHWA (1997b) for in-place recycling.
sections.body: If the recycled material simply replaces aggregate, the design steps of Section 2.3.2 apply; with geotextiles, Section 3.3.2 (p. 9-79). If the design charts are used (printed as Figures 9-2 or 9-7), an increased stabilization layer thickness is required for recycled material with CBR < 80; alternatively the Giroud and Han method in FHWA (2008) takes the material CBR as an input. Proof rolling should confirm thickness. For in-place recycling, step-by-step procedures are in FHWA (1997b).
key_points: Increase stabilization thickness for recycled material with CBR < 80 when using the design charts (p. 9-79).
sections.applicability: Sizing recycled aggregate stabilization layers.

sections.title: Primary Design References
sections.summary: Primary design references for recycled materials: FHWA (1997a) waste and byproduct guidelines, ARRA (2001) Basic Asphalt Recycling Manual and FHWA (1997b) pavement recycling guidelines.
sections.body: References (p. 9-79): FHWA (1997a), User Guidelines for Waste and Byproduct Materials in Pavement Construction (Chesner, Collins and MacKay, FHWA-RD-97-148); Asphalt Recycling and Reclaiming Association (ARRA) (2001), Basic Asphalt Recycling Manual; FHWA (1997b), Pavement Recycling Guidelines for State and Local Governments (Kandhal and Mallick, FHWA-SA-98-042).
sections.applicability: Finding design sources for recycled pavement materials.

sections.title: Overview of Construction Specifications and Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Specifications, quality assurance and monitoring for recycled aggregate stabilization layers. Subsections cover: Specification Development; Summary of Quality Assurance; Summary of Instrumentation Monitoring and Construction Control.
sections.body: This section covers specification development (5.4.1), quality assurance (5.4.2) and monitoring and construction control (5.4.3) for recycled stabilization (p. 9-79).
sections.applicability: Specifying and checking recycled stabilization layers.

sections.title: Specification Development
sections.summary: Specifications for RAP and RCP aggregates: state DOT aggregate specifications, the FHWA (1997a) user guidelines, and two university research center specifications (Edil 2011) with operator requirements for supply, compliance, safety and quality.
sections.body: RAP and RCP aggregates are essentially natural aggregates and most state DOTs have material, placement and compaction specifications (p. 9-79). FHWA (1997a) contains a Users Guideline section for RAP, RCM and other recycled fills (processing, properties, design, construction including cold weather and corrosion mitigation, unresolved issues); it and state specifications are reviewed in GeoTechTools (p. 9-80). A university recycled materials research center published two specifications for RAP and RCP as unbound road base (Edil 2011): a standard specification for grading requirements and density determination of RAP as unbound base and subbase (in ASTM balloting) and a standard guide for recycled aggregates as unbound roadbase (in draft). The guide assumes the operator (1) secures, stockpiles, crushes, tests and stockpiles the product; (2) complies with solid waste rules; (3) complies with air quality rules; (4) has worker health, safety and environmental plans; (5) meets recycled aggregate quality standards.
sections.applicability: Writing specifications for recycled stabilization aggregates.

sections.title: Summary of Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Quality control of recycled stabilization: moisture, density or stiffness and thickness, random stockpile sampling, segregation monitoring, GPS with point checks, DCP and proof rolling.
sections.body: As with gravel, primary quality control is moisture, density or stiffness and thickness (p. 9-80). Each recycled source differs, so random samples of stockpiles should be taken and stockpiling and handling monitored for segregation. GPS with point checks controls thickness; the DCP gives strength and effective depth; proof rolling evaluates deformation and rutting potential.
sections.applicability: Field quality checks on recycled aggregate layers.

sections.title: Summary of Instrumentation Monitoring and Construction Control
sections.summary: FWD testing from the surface of the improved layer measures layer and subgrade stiffness after in-place recycling, confirms design resilient modulus and gives a reference for long-term monitoring.
sections.body: The FWD test on the surface of the improved layer measures the stiffness of that layer and of the subgrade after in-place recycling (p. 9-81). Resilient modulus from FWD results confirms the design requirements and provides a reference for future FWD on the new pavement surface for long-term performance monitoring.
sections.applicability: Verifying recycled stabilization layers by FWD.

sections.title: Cost Data
sections.summary: Recycled pavement materials for stabilization are typically incorporated in highway reconstruction as subbase/base aggregate or roadbed embankment material.
sections.body: For stabilization applications, recycled pavement materials are typically incorporated into a highway reconstruction project, as aggregate in subbase/base courses or as roadbed embankment material (p. 9-81).
sections.applicability: Context for recycled material costs.

sections.title: Cost Components
sections.summary: Recycled material costs: specifications should allow but not force recycled materials; preliminary budgets should include a nominal saving of $2.00 to $5.00 per ton of recycled material used onsite, except very large projects over 100,000 tons.
sections.body: Specifications should allow the use of recycled materials but not force it, letting market forces set the most cost effective and sustainable use (p. 9-81). Availability of alternatives and demand from other markets strongly influence savings passed to the owner, making them hard to quantify. Except for very large projects (greater than 100,000 tons of available recycled material) where savings may be significant, preliminary budgets should include a nominal saving of $2.00 to $5.00 per ton of recycled material incorporated onsite. More cost information is on GeoTechTools.
key_points: Budget a nominal saving of $2.00 to $5.00 per ton of recycled material incorporated onsite (p. 9-81).
sections.applicability: Budgeting recycled material use in reconstruction.

sections.title: Admixture/Chemical Stabilization
sections.summary: Admixture (chemical) stabilization of pavement subgrades with cement, cement kiln dust, lime, fly ash, asphalt and combinations: overview of each admixture and a generic procedure for the optimum admixture content.
sections.body: A variety of admixtures can be mixed with the subgrade to improve its performance (p. 9-82). The section gives a general overview of each admixture and a generalized outline for determining the optimum admixture content, with references for the design details of each method.
sections.applicability: Chemical treatment of weak, plastic or wet pavement subgrades.

sections.title: Feasibility Considerations
sections.summary: Feasibility considerations for admixture stabilization: applications, advantages and disadvantages, geotechnical, environmental and site evaluations, limitations and alternatives.
sections.body: This section covers applications (6.1.1), advantages and disadvantages (6.1.2), feasibility evaluations (6.1.3), limitations (6.1.4) and alternatives (6.1.5) for admixture stabilization (pp. 9-82 to 9-88).
sections.applicability: Screening a subgrade for chemical stabilization.

sections.title: Applications
sections.summary: Applications of admixtures for soft, compressible, expansive and wet soils, the Austroads guide to selecting an admixture (Figure 9-8), cementing agents that bond particles and cut capillary passages, and caution with lime and lime-fly ash on clays in seasonal frost areas.
sections.body: Figure 9-8 (Austroads 1998) shows the admixture types with initial guidance on their application; forms of stabilization may be combined (e.g., lime to dry and reduce plasticity before another method), and miscellaneous chemicals are a broad guideline only (p. 9-82). Admixtures stabilize soft and/or compressible, expansive and wet soils (p. 9-83). Cementing agents (Portland cement, bitumen, lime, cement kiln dust and lime-fly ash) bond particles and partially remove capillary passages, reducing moisture movement. Care is needed with lime and lime-fly ash on clay soils in seasonal frost areas. For expansive soils, stabilization means treatment with bitumen, Portland cement, slaked or hydrated lime and fly ash to limit volume change; chemical stabilization can substantially increase strength.
key_points: Take care using lime and lime-fly ash with clay soils in seasonal frost areas (p. 9-83).
figures: Figure 9-8: Guide for selection of admixture stabilization method(s).
sections.applicability: Choosing an admixture type from soil grading and plasticity.

sections.title: Advantages and Potential Disadvantages
sections.summary: Heading for the advantages (9.6.1.2.1) and potential disadvantages (9.6.1.2.2) of admixture stabilization.
sections.body: Heading for the advantages and potential disadvantages of admixtures, 9.6.1.2.1 and 9.6.1.2.2; it has no text of its own. (p. 9-83)
sections.applicability: Weighing chemical stabilization against other methods.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.summary: Admixtures treat in place, avoiding over-excavation and disposal; they stiffen subgrades, reduce plasticity, water absorption, swell and compressibility, and raise strength and modulus with time; lime reduces swell by clay activity; some admixture suits most soils.
sections.body: Advantages: in-place treatment, eliminating over-excavated spoil and its disposal and replacement costs; increased subgrade stiffness; reduced plasticity, water absorption, swelling potential and compressibility, with strength and modulus rising over time; lime reduces swell in expansive soil more or less depending on the activity of the clay minerals; and admixtures exist for most soil types. (p. 9-83)
key_points: In-place treatment; no over-excavation or disposal (p. 9-83).
Strength and modulus increase with time (p. 9-83).
sections.applicability: Weighing chemical stabilization against other methods.

sections.title: Potential Disadvantages
sections.summary: Admixtures need several days to a week of curing, up-front lab testing and very good field control; dust and weather matter. Lime or fly ash can make a soil highly frost susceptible (reportedly from short curing), and sulfates can react with free lime in lime, CKD and possibly cement treatments to form expansive minerals.
sections.body: Admixtures usually need curing of several days, often up to one week, and adequate curing is important for strength gain. They need up-front laboratory testing and very good field control for a uniform, lasting product, and some methods raise dust and weather issues. Some treatments (e.g., lime or fly ash) can turn a soil with negligible to moderate frost heave into one highly frost susceptible, behaving more like silt; for lime this has been reported as caused by insufficient curing ('was been caused', as printed). With lime, CKD and possibly cement, sulfates in the soil could react with free lime to form expansive minerals and new swelling (p. 9-84). (pp. 9-83 to 9-84)
key_points: Curing of several days, often up to one week (p. 9-83).
Lime or fly ash may make soil highly frost susceptible (p. 9-83).
Sulfates with free lime form expansive minerals (p. 9-84).
sections.applicability: Weighing chemical stabilization against other methods.

sections.title: Feasibility Evaluations
sections.summary: Heading for geotechnical, environmental and site feasibility of admixture stabilization (9.6.1.3.1 to 9.6.1.3.3).
sections.body: Heading for the feasibility evaluations of admixture stabilization, 9.6.1.3.1 to 9.6.1.3.3; it has no text of its own. (p. 9-84)
sections.applicability: Checking whether cement or lime suits a subgrade soil.

sections.title: Geotechnical
sections.summary: Cement: PI < 20 and at least 45% passing No. 40 (or pretreat plastic clays with lime or fly ash); 3 to 10% cement for granular soils with at least 150 psi in 7 days; AASHTO M 85; 95% of AASHTO T 134. Lime: 3 to 8% for plastic clays with at least 50 psi in 28 days; PI about 10 lower limit; 95% of AASHTO T 99.
sections.body: Table 9-2 and Figure 9-8 give each admixture's applicability. For cement, proper mixing needs PI less than 20 and at least 45% passing the No. 40 sieve, though highly plastic clays pretreated with lime or fly ash may then take cement. For granular and/or nonplastic soils, cement is 3 to 10% of dry soil weight with an unconfined strength of at least 150 psi within 7 days; cement meets AASHTO M 85, and the layer is compacted to at least 95% of AASHTO T 134. For lime stabilization of clays or highly plastic clayey soils, lime is 3 to 8% of dry weight with at least 50 psi within 28 days; the optimum content comes from unconfined strength and Atterberg limit tests on mixes at varying lime contents, with pH giving the initial near-optimum value. Pozzolanic gain depends on the soil's silica and alumina; plasticity is a rough guide, and a plasticity index of about 10 is commonly the lower limit for inorganic clays. The lime layer is compacted to at least 95% of AASHTO T 99. Pozzolanic fly ash suits cohesive and granular materials; asphalt suits silty, sandy and granular materials. (p. 9-84)
key_points: Cement: PI < 20, >= 45% passing No. 40; 3-10%, >= 150 psi in 7 days (p. 9-84).
Lime: 3-8%, >= 50 psi in 28 days; PI about 10 lower limit (p. 9-84).
Compaction: 95% of AASHTO T 134 (cement), T 99 (lime) (p. 9-84).
sections.applicability: Checking whether cement or lime suits a subgrade soil.

sections.title: Environmental Considerations
sections.summary: Dust control and weather are the important environmental considerations in choosing admixture methods.
sections.body: As noted under the disadvantages, dust control and weather are important environmental considerations in selecting these technologies. (p. 9-84)
key_points: Dust control and weather govern (p. 9-84).
sections.applicability: Checking whether cement or lime suits a subgrade soil.

sections.title: Site Conditions
sections.summary: Two agencies' selection aids (Figure 9-9 graph; Figures 9-10, 9-11 flowcharts, including sulfate-rich soils) with Table 9-2 and Figure 9-8: evaluate classification, moisture, plasticity, sulfate and organic content and strength, and the water table, since high water may need dewatering.
sections.body: The graph in Figure 9-9 (cement or lime stabilization) and the flowcharts in Figures 9-10 (first-level strategy) and 9-11 (sulfate-rich soils) summarize the site conditions two agencies (Ohio DOT and Caltrans) use to select admixture strategies (pp. 9-85 to 9-87). With Table 9-2 and Figure 9-8, the conditions to evaluate are classification, moisture content, plasticity, sulfate content, organic content and strength of the soils; the water table should also be located, since high water may impede construction and require dewatering. (pp. 9-85 to 9-87)
key_points: Selection aids: Figures 9-9 to 9-11 (pp. 9-85 to 9-87).
Evaluate classification, moisture, plasticity, sulfates, organics, strength (p. 9-87).
figures: Figure 9-9: Site conditions for considering cement or lime stabilization.
Figure 9-10: Selecting a first-level project subgrade stabilization strategy.
Figure 9-11: Selection of stabilization strategy for sulfate-rich soils.
sections.applicability: Checking whether cement or lime suits a subgrade soil.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.summary: Limitations of admixtures: soils too soft for mixing equipment (CBR < 1), stabilization generally not required when PI < 12 and R > 20, no cementitious or pozzolanic stabilization above 8000 ppm sulfate, special strategies above 3000 ppm, and reduced effect with organics.
sections.body: A main limitation is soils too soft to support mixing equipment (p. 9-87). If PI is less than 12 and R > 20, stabilization is generally not required; if CBR < 1 (R < 1) the subgrade will likely not support mixing equipment and other technologies (geosynthetics, lightweight fill) should be considered. The other primary limitation is sulfates: cementitious and pozzolanic stabilization should not be used when soil sulfate content exceeds 8000 ppm (Figure 9-10), and special strategies are needed above 3000 ppm (Figure 9-11), with swell tests. Organics reduce the effectiveness of cementitious and pozzolanic methods, requiring significant increases in quantity if they work at all (p. 9-88).
key_points: Stabilization is generally not required if PI < 12 and R > 20 (p. 9-87).
With CBR < 1 the subgrade likely will not support admixture mixing equipment.
No cementitious or pozzolanic stabilization above 8000 ppm sulfate; special strategies and swell tests above 3000 ppm.
sections.applicability: Recognizing soils where chemical stabilization should not be used.

sections.title: Alternative Solutions (or Technologies)
sections.summary: Alternatives to admixtures: more gravel, geosynthetics with gravel, dewatering, lightweight fill for soils too soft for admixtures, and partial encapsulation for swelling soils.
sections.body: More gravel, geosynthetics with gravel and/or dewatering are standard alternatives to admixtures for weak soils (p. 9-88). Geosynthetics and lightweight fill are especially effective where soils are too soft for admixtures. For swelling soils, partial encapsulation could be considered (printed as covered in Section 8 Moisture Control).
sections.applicability: Choosing a non-chemical alternative.

sections.title: Construction and Materials
sections.summary: Construction steps and admixture materials for chemical stabilization: construction of chemical stabilization: delivery and distribution, mixing (poor mixing the leading cause of failure), compaction and curing above 40°F for 3 to 7 days; dry hydrated lime, quicklime or slurry; two-stage mixing for plastic clays; lime lowering maximum density.
sections.body: This section covers construction (6.2.1) and the admixture materials: cement and CKD, lime, fly ash, asphalt and combinations (6.2.2) (pp. 9-88 to 9-94).
sections.applicability: Building chemically stabilized subgrades.

sections.title: Construction
sections.summary: Construction of chemical stabilization: delivery and distribution, mixing (poor mixing the leading cause of failure), compaction and curing above 40°F for 3 to 7 days; dry hydrated lime, quicklime or slurry; two-stage mixing for plastic clays; lime lowering maximum density.
sections.body: The basic steps are (1) pozzolan delivery and distribution, (2) mixing, (3) compacting and (4) curing (p. 9-88). Pozzolans are applied dry or as slurry; dry hydrated lime is very fine and dusty, quicklime granular and much less dusty. Material is spread by hand from bags, pneumatic trucks with spreader bars or dump trucks with controlled tailgates; lime slurry is mixed centrally or in portable systems, typically 1 ton of lime with 500 gallons of water giving a slurry with 31% lime solids (TRB 1987; the printed text says 600 tons of slurry). Adequate mixing is critical; poor mixing is the leading cause of unsatisfactory results; soils are mixed by disking, repeated blading or traveling rotary or pug-mill mixers, in thin lifts with multiple passes. Highly plastic materials may be mixed in two stages, the reduced plasticity after several days of curing aiding final mixing. Compaction follows standard procedures, but lime generally decreases maximum density and increases optimum water content, so compaction curves of the in situ mixture may be needed for control (p. 9-89). Curing above 40°F with adequate moisture is essential for pozzolanic strength gain; 3 to 7 days is typical, with moist curing or an asphalt seal. Final evaluation is by proof rolling, DCP and/or FWD.
key_points: Poor mixing is the leading cause of unsatisfactory stabilization results (p. 9-88).
Lime generally lowers maximum density and raises optimum water content; use compaction curves of the in situ mixture (p. 9-89).
Cure above 40°F with adequate moisture; a 3 to 7 day cure is typical.
sections.applicability: Field construction of lime, cement and fly ash treated subgrades.

sections.title: Materials
sections.summary: Heading for admixture materials: Portland cement and CKD, lime, fly ash, asphalt and combinations (9.6.2.2.1 to 9.6.2.2.5).
sections.body: Heading for the admixture materials, 9.6.2.2.1 to 9.6.2.2.5; it has no text of its own. (p. 9-89)
sections.applicability: Selecting and qualifying cement, lime, fly ash and asphalt admixtures.

sections.title: Portland Cement and Cement Kiln Dust (CKD)
sections.summary: Type II cement has largely replaced Type I for sulfate resistance; Type III may be stronger (ASTM C150). Organics retard hydration: pH of a 10:1 soil-cement mix at least 12.0 after 15 minutes suggests no interference. Avoid cement for fine-grained soils with more than about 1% sulfate; report CKD sulfates and swell-test if present.
sections.body: Several cement types work: Type I and Type IA gave about the same results; Type II has largely replaced Type I for greater sulfate resistance at similar cost; Type III (high early strength, finer, different composition) gives higher strength in some soils; specifications are in ASTM C150. Organic matter and/or sulfates can harm soil cement and should be tested for if suspected. Organics: soils may be acid, neutral or alkaline; undecomposed vegetation may be harmless, but low molecular weight compounds (nucleic acid, dextrose) retard hydration; if the pH of a 10:1 soil-cement mixture (dry weight) 15 minutes after mixing is at least 12.0, organics probably will not interfere. Sulfates (p. 9-90): sulfate-clay reactions can deteriorate fine-grained soil-cement, while granular soil-cements seem unaffected (small amounts may even help); sulfate-resistant cement may not help clay soils but may help granular soil-cements exposed to sulfate-rich soil or groundwater; cement for fine-grained soils with more than about 1% sulfate should be avoided. For CKD, sulfates in the CKD or soil may react with free lime and swell, so CKD sulfate content must be reported, soils tested for sulfate minerals (often gypsum), and swell tests run if sulfates are present. (pp. 9-89 to 9-90)
key_points: Type II has largely replaced Type I for sulfate resistance (p. 9-89).
10:1 soil-cement pH >= 12.0 after 15 min: organics probably harmless (p. 9-89).
Avoid cement in fine-grained soils with more than about 1% sulfate (p. 9-90).
sections.applicability: Selecting and qualifying cement, lime, fly ash and asphalt admixtures.

sections.title: Lime
sections.summary: Hydrated lime is most used, quicklime growing; both and dolomitic forms come from calcining limestone or dolomite. Lime dries the soil, its Ca and Mg cations exchange for Na and K, cutting plasticity, swell and shrink, and agglomerates particles toward silt or sand texture, within about 1 hour with thorough mixing (Figure 9-12).
sections.body: Common soil stabilization limes are hydrated lime [Ca(OH)2], quicklime [CaO] and their dolomitic forms [Ca(OH)2.MgO and CaO.MgO]. Hydrated lime remains most used in the United States, though use of the more caustic quicklime has grown over the past two decades. Lime is made by calcining limestone or dolomite below the melting point to decompose carbonates; some by-product lime is more variable and poorer. Figure 9-12 (p. 9-91) shows typical effects of lime on natural soils. Hydration absorbs soil water, drying it at once; calcium (Ca+2) and magnesium (Mg+2) cations exchange with sodium (Na+) and potassium (K+), reducing plasticity and usually swell and shrinkage and moisture-related strength loss, and improving workability; particles agglomerate, and plastic clays become more like silt or sand in texture. These effects occur very rapidly, usually within 1 hour, with thorough mixing (p. 9-92). (pp. 9-90 to 9-92)
key_points: Hydrated lime most used; quicklime use growing (p. 9-90).
Cation exchange reduces plasticity, swell and shrinkage (p. 9-92).
Drying and texture effects within about 1 hour with thorough mixing (p. 9-92).
figures: Figure 9-12: Examples of the effects of lime stabilization on various soils.
sections.applicability: Selecting and qualifying cement, lime, fly ash and asphalt admixtures.

sections.title: Fly Ash
sections.summary: Class C fly ash (lignite or subbituminous, high lime) is self-cementing and pozzolanic; Class F (anthracite or bituminous, low lime) needs lime; stabilization ash must meet ASTM C593 'for Class C fly ash' (as printed); with lime and water its silicon and aluminum compounds harden to high strength.
sections.body: Fly ash (coal ash) is the mineral residue of burning pulverized coal, classed by coal type. Class C, from lignite or subbituminous coal, is 'high lime' ash, self-reactive or cementitious with water as well as pozzolanic. Class F, from anthracite or bituminous coal, is 'low lime' ash and needs added lime for a pozzolanic reaction. As printed, fly ash for stabilization must meet ASTM C593 'for Class C fly ash'. Its silicon and aluminum compounds with lime and water form a hardened cementitious mass of high compressive strength. (p. 9-92)
key_points: Class C self-cementing; Class F needs lime (p. 9-92).
Must meet ASTM C593 (p. 9-92).
sections.applicability: Selecting and qualifying cement, lime, fly ash and asphalt admixtures.

sections.title: Asphalt
sections.summary: Asphalt suits silty, sandy and granular soils, used up to PI 15 but mostly on well-graded low-fines sands, as a binder and void filler giving a flexible platform and some moisture resistance (not in poorly drained areas); in-place work uses emulsions rather than cutbacks.
sections.body: Asphalt stabilization suits silty, sandy and granular materials; it has been used on soils with plasticity indices up to 15 but more commonly on sandy, well-graded soils with low fines, giving a relatively flexible platform. Asphalt binds and fills or partly fills voids, giving some moisture resistance but is not appropriate in poorly drained areas. It reduces permeability by increasing path tortuosity, which can make a waterproof surface over water sensitive soils if combined with the geometric design into a system (p. 9-93); reduced voids may shift shear volume change from contractive to dilative. Most bituminous stabilization is in place, bitumen applied to the soil and mixed and compacted at once, with liquid asphalts (emulsions); emulsions are preferred to cutbacks, which many agencies no longer allow. (pp. 9-92 to 9-93)
key_points: Used up to PI 15; mostly well-graded low-fines sands (p. 9-92).
Not appropriate in poorly drained areas (p. 9-92).
Emulsions preferred; cutbacks often not allowed (p. 9-93).
sections.applicability: Selecting and qualifying cement, lime, fly ash and asphalt admixtures.

sections.title: Combinations
sections.summary: In combinations one stabilizer makes up for another: lime first cuts clay plasticity so cement or asphalt can mix. Lime-cement: minimum lime for workability and PI. Lime-asphalt: about 1 to 2% lime as anti-stripping agent. Lime-fly ash: matrix (fly ash, lime, minus No. 4 fines) about 2% above the optimum fines content.
sections.body: Combination stabilizers let one stabilizer compensate for another's weakness; in clay areas without base material, lime has been used with Portland cement or asphalt for base courses, added first to reduce plasticity since cement or asphalt cannot be mixed into plastic clay; costlier than single stabilizers but economical where base aggregate is expensive. Lime-cement: lime as initial additive or primary stabilizer, mainly to improve workability by reducing plasticity; the design lime content is the minimum giving the desired results. Lime-asphalt: lime improves workability and acts as an anti-stripping agent, neutralizing acidic chemicals that hinder bonding; about 1 to 2 percent lime usually suffices, and asphalt procedures govern. Lime-fly ash: lime-fly ash percentage, moisture and lime to fly ash ratio are varied (p. 9-94); strength and durability depend on the matrix (fly ash, lime and minus No. 4 fines), best when it 'floats' the coarse aggregate. The matrix quantity for maximum dry density is the optimum fines content, and about 2 percent above it is recommended; the lime-fly ash ratio then tunes strength and durability. (pp. 9-93 to 9-94)
key_points: Lime added first to reduce clay plasticity (p. 9-93).
Lime-asphalt: about 1 to 2% lime as anti-stripping agent (p. 9-93).
Lime-fly ash: matrix about 2% above optimum fines content (p. 9-94).

sections.title: Design Overview
sections.summary: Design overview for admixture stabilization: binder selection and a generic mix design procedure. Subsections cover: Design Considerations (Chemical/Binder Selection); Design Steps; Primary Design References.
sections.body: This section covers design considerations for chemical and binder selection (6.3.1), generic design steps (6.3.2) and primary design references (6.3.3) (pp. 9-94 to 9-96).
sections.applicability: Designing chemically stabilized subgrades.

sections.title: Design Considerations (Chemical/Binder Selection)
sections.summary: Admixture design depends on the purpose (reduce moisture, reduce plasticity, improve strength) with special consideration of sulfate, organic, pH and chloride contents; Jones et al. (2010) give detailed steps.
sections.body: Design of the admixture depends on the purpose of stabilization: reducing moisture content, reducing plasticity or improving strength (p. 9-94). Special consideration must be given to the sulfate content, organic content, pH and chloride content of the soil, which could affect performance and durability. Jones et al. (2010) provides detailed design steps for each issue.
sections.applicability: Choosing a binder for a stabilization purpose.

sections.title: Design Steps
sections.summary: Generic nine-step mix design for lime, cement, lime-fly ash, lime-cement-fly ash or asphalt: classify, select admixture and trial mixes (lime at pH about 12.4 in 1 hour), moisture-density, cured triplicates, strength, resilient modulus, freeze-thaw, select content, and add 0.5 to 1%.
sections.body: For improving subgrade strength the design is generic to lime, cement, lime-fly ash, lime-cement-fly ash or asphalt (p. 9-94). Step 1: classify the soil (% < No. 200, % < No. 40, PI, sulfate content). Step 2: select admixture(s) (Table 9-2, Figures 9-9 to 9-12) and prepare trial mixes (FHWA 2010, JDAAF 1994, Jones et al. 2010): lime, select the lowest % with pH about 12.4 in 1 hour; cement, estimate content from a table; asphalt, use the equation and table in FHWA 2010 or JDAAF 1994 (p. 9-95). Step 3: develop the moisture-density relationship. Step 4: prepare triplicate samples cured at the specified density (e.g., 90% AASHTO T 180 or ASTM D1557) at optimum water and admixture contents several points above and below. Step 5: index strength, unconfined compressive strength (ASTM D5102 or AASHTO T 208) for lime and cement, Marshall Stability (ASTM D6927 or AASHTO T 245) for asphalt. Step 6: resilient modulus (e.g., AASHTO T 307) at the optimum, tested or correlated. Step 7: freeze-thaw tests as regionally required for cement, cement-fly ash, lime-cement-fly ash. Step 8: select the percent meeting minimum design strength and freeze-thaw durability. Step 9: add 0.5 to 1% to compensate for non-uniform mixing.
key_points: Lime trial: select the lowest % giving pH about 12.4 in 1 hour (p. 9-94).
Cure triplicate specimens at the specified density, e.g., 90% AASHTO T 180 (p. 9-95).
Add 0.5 to 1% admixture to compensate for non-uniform mixing.
sections.applicability: Running a laboratory mix design for a chemically stabilized subgrade.

sections.summary: Primary design references for admixture stabilization: JDAAF (1994) TM 5-822-14, FHWA (2010), Jones et al. (2010), National Lime Association (2004), Portland Cement Association (1995), American Coal Ash Association (1991) and Asphalt Institute (1979).

(2010) guidelines for the stabilization of subgrade soils; National Lime Association (2004) Lime-Treated Soil Construction Manual; Portland Cement Association (1995) Soil-Cement Construction Handbook; American Coal Ash Association (1991) Flexible Pavement Manual; Asphalt Institute (1979) A Basic Emulsion Manual.

sections.title: Overview of Construction Specifications and Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Specifications, quality assurance and monitoring for chemically stabilized subgrades. Subsections cover: Specification Development; Summary of Quality Assurance; Summary of Instrumentation Monitoring and Construction Control.
sections.body: This section covers specification development (6.4.1), quality assurance (6.4.2) and monitoring and construction control (6.4.3) for admixture stabilization (pp. 9-96 to 9-97).
sections.applicability: Specifying and checking chemical stabilization.

sections.title: Specification Development
sections.summary: Combined performance and method specifications for chemical stabilization: acceptance criteria, contractor qualifications and responsibilities, resilient modulus and durability requirements, and an outline from grade correction and test strip to curing and trafficking.
sections.body: Combined performance and method approach specifications are used for most chemical stabilization projects (p. 9-96). They should include acceptance criteria and minimum contractor qualifications, state the contractor's responsibility for material selection, mix design and quality control, identify equipment and construction methods, and define the engineer's responsibility for mix design verification and quality assurance. Stabilized materials should meet specified resilient modulus and durability requirements; sulfate-rich and organic soils need special considerations. General requirements: grade correction, test strip, mixing and application equipment, mixing crew responsibilities, mixing depth and moisture content, mellowing before compaction (lime), compaction, compaction quality control, curing and trafficking (p. 9-97). All vehicles should be kept off the stabilized layer during the curing period and/or until the minimum specified strength is reached.
key_points: Keep all vehicles off the stabilized layer during curing and/or until the minimum specified strength is achieved (p. 9-97).
sections.applicability: Writing specifications for chemical subgrade stabilization.

sections.title: Summary of Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Quality assurance of chemical stabilization: agency mix design verification, measurement of thickness, moisture, stabilizer content, compaction and delay, curing, gradation, strength and modulus, and blend uniformity checked in test holes with phenolphthalein for lime and cement.
sections.body: The agency should verify the mix design and conduct quality assurance unless the contract assigns it to others (p. 9-97). Critical parameters are thickness of the stabilized layer, moisture content, stabilizer content, compaction effort and delay, curing procedures and time, gradation of the mixture, shear strength and modulus. Blend uniformity is one of the more important measures: dig holes across the roadway and check for uniform consistency, color and moisture, sampling for moisture and, if possible, stabilizer content. For cement and lime, spraying the hole sides with phenolphthalein gives a quick check; the soil should turn a uniform deep red, indicating sufficient stabilizer.
key_points: Phenolphthalein sprayed in test holes should turn lime or cement treated soil a uniform deep red (p. 9-97).
sections.applicability: Field quality checks on chemically treated subgrades.

sections.title: Summary of Instrumentation Monitoring and Construction Control
sections.summary: Monitoring chemical stabilization: thickness and uniformity from test holes, DCP and ground penetrating radar (ASTM D6432), and FWD or LFWD backcalculated resilient modulus for compliance and long-term reference.
sections.body: Thickness and blend uniformity are best measured with test holes along and across the alignment, complemented by DCP and/or ground penetrating radar (GPR, ASTM D6432) (p. 9-97). Performance monitoring could include FWD or LFWD to confirm design compliance and gather data; the backcalculated resilient modulus confirms design requirements and is a reference for future FWD on the new pavement surface.
sections.applicability: Verifying chemically stabilized layers.

sections.title: Cost Data
sections.summary: Cost data for chemical stabilization of subgrades: chemical stabilization costs (2007 to 2010 data): subgrade modification pay item by the square yard at $2 to $5 (printed per cubic yard) for projects over 10,000 yd2; cement and lime $100 to $150/ton over 150 tons; fly ash $40 to $80/ton over 350 tons; mixing plant mobilization about $25,000.
sections.body: This section gives the cost components for chemical subgrade stabilization (p. 9-98).
sections.applicability: Estimating chemical stabilization cost.

sections.title: Cost Components
sections.summary: Chemical stabilization costs (2007 to 2010 data): subgrade modification pay item by the square yard at $2 to $5 (printed per cubic yard) for projects over 10,000 yd2; cement and lime $100 to $150/ton over 150 tons; fly ash $40 to $80/ton over 350 tons; mixing plant mobilization about $25,000.
sections.body: Typical pay items are subgrade modification by the square yard (equipment, labor and incidentals to mix, compact and fine grade) and cement, fly ash or lime by the ton (p. 9-98). Bid prices for subgrade modification on projects over 10,000 yd2 range from $2 to $5 (printed as per cubic yard). Material prices: cement $100 to $150 per ton for quantities > 150 tons; fly ash $40 to $80 per ton for > 350 tons; lime $100 to $150 per ton for > 150 tons. Most equipment is common to highway work so added mobilization is negligible, except an on-site plant for a chemically modified base, about $25,000 to mobilize. Cost ranges are based on 2007 through 2010 data; see GeoTechTools.
key_points: Cement and lime $100 to $150 per ton (> 150 tons); fly ash $40 to $80 per ton (> 350 tons) (p. 9-98).
Mobilization of an on-site mixing plant is about $25,000.
sections.applicability: Pricing chemical subgrade stabilization.

sections.title: Moisture Control: Improved Drainage - Dewatering
sections.summary: Moisture control by drainage and dewatering for subgrade stabilization: deep drains and underdrains, edgedrains, drainage blankets and capillary breaks, with AASHTO (1993) allowing up to half the base thickness for excellent versus poor drainage.
sections.body: Section 7.0 (pp. 9-99 to 9-111) covers drainage and dewatering to stabilize wet, saturated subgrades: feasibility, construction and materials, design steps with Eqs. 9-9 to 9-14, specifications and quality assurance, and cost.
sections.applicability: Stabilizing wet subgrades by drainage, temporarily for construction or permanently.

sections.title: Feasibility Considerations
sections.summary: Why drainage stabilizes subgrades: most soils needing stabilization are wet and saturated; deep drains and underdrains (typically deeper than 3 ft), edgedrains, drainage blankets and capillary breaks; AASHTO (1993) base thickness reduction up to a factor of 2 with excellent drainage.
sections.body: Most soils require stabilization because they are wet and saturated; drainage as part of subgrade stabilization has significant construction benefits and, if permanent, long-term benefits (p. 9-99). Deep drains and underdrains, typically greater than 3 feet deep, remove and control groundwater and can be combined with or built as edgedrains to remove infiltration. Drainable stabilization layers can be drainage blankets connected to underdrains and edgedrains or daylighted at the ditch line, or capillary breaks intercepting rising capillary water and vapor. Drainage strongly influences pavement design: in high rainfall areas, per AASHTO (1993), the base of a flexible pavement (relatively thick base) can be reduced in thickness by as much as a factor of 2, or the design life extended equivalently, with excellent rather than poor drainage; improved drainage also reduces rigid slab thickness. The MEPDG (AASHTO 2008) does not evaluate drainage directly but assumes good to excellent drainage.
key_points: Deep drains and underdrains are typically greater than 3 ft deep (p. 9-99).
AASHTO (1993): excellent versus poor drainage can halve the base thickness of a flexible pavement in high rainfall areas.
The MEPDG assumes good to excellent drainage has been incorporated.
sections.applicability: Deciding whether drainage can stabilize a wet subgrade.

sections.title: Applications
sections.summary: When to use subgrade drains: high groundwater, spring thaw and springs, silts and very fine sands, seeps, poor drainage signs, rubblization or full depth reclamation, wet climates; trench, blanket and interceptor drains, well points, drains holding water more than 5 ft below subgrade, and drained capillary barriers.
sections.body: Consider subgrade drains where there are high groundwater, spring thaw bleeding or springs; silts and very fine sands that become quick or spongy when saturated; seeps from water-bearing strata or cuts (intercepting drains); signs of poor drainage in existing pavements; a subgrade to be stabilized for rubblization or full depth reclamation; and wet climates (pp. 9-99 to 9-100). Seepage is controlled by longitudinal or transverse drains, deep trench drains or graded filter blanket drains (e.g., a granular stabilization layer) (Cedergren 1989); interceptor trench drains on sloping terrain; well points or deep horizontal drains for extremely wet soils; storm drain or sump connection where drains cannot daylight. For frost susceptible soils use deep horizontal drains below the freezing front. Keeping free water more than 5 feet below the subgrade surface usually controls capillary rise (Cedergren 1989). A capillary barrier (filter/separation layer, open graded gravel or cobbles, filter/separation layer) also gives a stabilization platform; it must be above the water table, below the freezing front and drained. Retrofitted edge drainage can improve subgrades of existing pavements; functioning underdrains typically reduce pumping within a few days.
key_points: Drains keeping free water more than 5 ft below the subgrade surface usually control capillary rise (p. 9-100).
A capillary barrier must be above the water table, below the freezing front and drained.
Underdrains typically reduce subgrade pumping within a few days once functioning.
sections.applicability: Selecting a drainage layout for a wet or frost-susceptible subgrade.

sections.title: Advantages and Potential Disadvantages
sections.summary: Heading for the advantages (9.7.1.2.1) and potential disadvantages (9.7.1.2.2) of drains for subgrade stabilization.
sections.body: Heading for the advantages and potential disadvantages of drainage, 9.7.1.2.1 and 9.7.1.2.2; it has no text of its own. (p. 9-100)
sections.applicability: Weighing drainage stabilization.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.summary: Drains are well established, fast and easy to install with light equipment even on very poor subgrades, cheap before construction with large savings if dewatering works, can reduce pavement design or extend life, renew facilities rapidly with little traffic disruption, and keep lower layers from saturating.
sections.body: Advantages: a well-established technology and common practice; drains are relatively fast and easy to install with readily available, relatively light equipment, with access even over very poor subgrades (p. 9-101); they can be installed before construction at relatively low cost, with substantial savings if dewatering succeeds; effective drainage can reduce pavement design requirements and/or extend life; they renew facilities rapidly with minimal traffic disruption; and they prevent saturation of underlying layers, speeding construction. (pp. 9-100 to 9-101)
key_points: Fast, easy installation with light equipment (p. 9-101).
Low cost before construction; savings if dewatering succeeds (p. 9-101).
sections.applicability: Weighing drainage stabilization.

sections.title: Potential Disadvantages
sections.summary: Drain effectiveness and timing are hard to predict, since permeability is uncertain within an order of magnitude (weeks, not days); the AASHTO MEPDG gives drainage no credit; drains depend on careful construction, need maintenance, and on contaminated sites need permits.
sections.body: Effectiveness of drains is hard to predict, especially the time for improvement: permeability and flow are hard to predict within an order of magnitude (weeks instead of days). The AASHTO MEPDG (AASHTO 2008) does not credit drainage in pavement design, so long-term cost-benefit cannot readily be evaluated. Drains rely heavily on careful construction and can be compromised by it, need maintenance (cleaning drains and outlets) during and after construction, and draining contaminated sites will likely require permits. (p. 9-101)
key_points: Time for improvement uncertain within an order of magnitude (p. 9-101).
AASHTO MEPDG gives no credit for drainage (p. 9-101).
sections.applicability: Weighing drainage stabilization.

sections.title: Feasibility Evaluations
sections.summary: Heading for geotechnical, environmental and site feasibility of drainage stabilization (9.7.1.3.1 to 9.7.1.3.3).
sections.body: Heading for the feasibility evaluations of drainage stabilization, 9.7.1.3.1 to 9.7.1.3.3; it has no text of its own. (p. 9-101)
