sections.title: Geotechnical
sections.summary: Identify saturated strata, groundwater depth and flow between strata, especially at cut-fill transitions and in cuts; subsurface water weakens base and subgrade and magnifies expansive soil movement. Soils not free draining above 80-90% saturation within 2 to 4 ft of the surface will not carry construction traffic.
sections.body: Identify saturated strata, groundwater depth and water flow between strata, especially at transitions between cut and fill. Water saturating unbound base/subbase and subgrade can greatly reduce strength and stiffness, causing premature depressions, rutting or cracking, and seasonal flow through strata can magnify differential volume change in expansive soils; cut areas are particularly critical. Soils subject to significant deformation and not free draining (saturation above 80 - 90%) within 2 to 4 feet of the surface are not expected to support construction traffic (p. 9-102). (pp. 9-101 to 9-102)
key_points: Cut-fill transitions and cuts are critical for subsurface water (p. 9-101).
Above 80-90% saturation within 2 to 4 ft: no construction traffic (p. 9-102).
sections.applicability: Investigating a site for drainage stabilization.

sections.title: Environmental Considerations
sections.summary: Wet weather may delay improvement, but drained sites resume work much sooner after rain; contaminated sites need permits and testing of drain water, and trench spoil disposal is harder there.
sections.body: Wet weather affects performance and may delay subgrade improvement, though drained sites will likely resume construction much sooner after rain. Contaminated sites need special permits and testing of water leaving the drains, and drain trench spoil disposal is even more of a problem there. (p. 9-102)
key_points: Drained sites resume work sooner after rain (p. 9-102).
Contaminated sites need permits and water testing (p. 9-102).
sections.applicability: Investigating a site for drainage stabilization.

sections.title: Site Conditions
sections.summary: Signs that underdrains are needed: clogged outlets, free water, water bodies above or below, saturated moderately permeable soils, seepage in layers, test pits or cuts, water on rock undercuts, and in wet climates subgrade permeability below 10 ft/day. Measure piezometric levels along and across the site to plan collection and discharge.
sections.body: Conditions indicating underdrains: existing underdrains with clogged outlets on rehabilitation projects; free water in the subgrade; water bodies or watersheds above and/or below the site; saturated soils of moderately high permeability (sandy silt, silty clay, low plasticity silt); groundwater seepage through permeable layers; water seeping into test pits or from higher ground in cuts; water flowing on top of rock undercuts; and, in wet climates, subgrade permeability less than 10 feet/day, where subsurface drainage or other moisture measures should be considered. Identify surface and groundwater sources and flow paths by measuring piezometric levels along and across the site; with topography this decides where to collect and discharge water. (p. 9-102)
key_points: Wet climates, subgrade permeability below 10 ft/day: consider subsurface drainage (p. 9-102).
Measure piezometric levels along and across the site (p. 9-102).
sections.applicability: Investigating a site for drainage stabilization.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.summary: Limitations of drainage stabilization: large wide flat areas are hard to drain, saturated soils with more than 10% fines are not drainable for construction traffic without significant time, and contaminated discharge may need permits or be disallowed.
sections.body: Limitations include: large wide flat areas are difficult to drain because surface infiltration exposure and inflow gradients are large while discharge areas and gradients are small (Cedergren 1989); saturated soils with more than 10% fines (minus No. 200) are not expected to be drainable for construction traffic unless significant time is available; discharge from contaminated sites requires special permits and may not be allowed (p. 9-103).
key_points: Saturated soils with more than 10% fines are not expected to drain enough for construction traffic without significant time (p. 9-103).
sections.applicability: Recognizing where drainage will not stabilize a subgrade in time.

sections.title: Construction and Materials
sections.summary: Construction of temporary and permanent drains for stabilization: cleaning existing outlets on rehabilitation projects, centerline construction underdrains with porous backfill to subgrade, and sacrificial construction underdrains.
sections.body: Whether drains are temporary for construction or part of the permanent pavement, proper construction is critical, and contractor and inspector should know how each activity affects drainage performance (p. 9-103). Significant stability improvement comes from cleaning existing underdrain outlets on rehabilitation projects and adding underdrains on new projects; on phased projects the contractor should clean outlets for the whole project at once. New projects allow longer drainage time; the start of construction and before winter shutdown are opportune. Construction underdrains are usually on the roadway centerline, or in the ditch line where water enters from a higher cut; porous backfill extends to subgrade elevation; outlets use the same pipe and backfill as regular underdrains and may discharge to catch basins, manholes, pipes or ditches. Contamination of the upper backfill is not a concern: construction underdrains are sacrificial and keep working through and after the contract (p. 9-104).
key_points: Clean outlets for the whole project at once on phased rehabilitation projects (p. 9-103).
Construction underdrains are sacrificial and keep working even with contaminated upper backfill (p. 9-104).
sections.applicability: Installing drains to stabilize subgrades during construction.

sections.title: Construction
sections.summary: Construction of drains: proper grade without undulations, connection to drainage layers and outlets, protecting shallow pipes from heavy traffic, filters around backfill, compacted bedding below the pipe invert, keeping backfill unfouled, headwalls and inspection before acceptance.
sections.body: Proper grading is essential; undulating drain lines are not acceptable (p. 9-104). Drains must connect to drainage layers (stabilization, base) and outlets set at proper grades with graded ditch lines. Mark drain lines and keep concrete trucks and heavy equipment off shallow lines; permanent drains are sometimes installed after paving; temporary drainage should be maintained until permanent drains exist to avoid a bathtub effect. Place the filter (geotextile or aggregate) around all sides of the backfill without blocking flow from an open graded base; backfill at least as permeable as the permeable base. Most states use graded aggregate, some free-draining sand; place and compact drainage backfill below the pipe invert to support the pipe and prevent subsidence; place the pipe at grade on a level surface; protect backfill from fouling (a shovel full of fines could clog the drain), keep construction traffic off and consider a geotextile cover; keep outlets draining, maintain ditches, install headwalls and mark outlets. Inspect and test the system near the end of construction, before final acceptance.
key_points: Undulating drain lines are not acceptable (p. 9-104).
Backfill drains with material at least as permeable as the permeable base.
Keep construction traffic off drain lines; a shovel full of fines could clog the drain.
sections.applicability: Field construction of trench drains and underdrains.

sections.title: Materials
sections.summary: Drain materials: aggregate in trench drains and drainage blankets must meet both filtration compatibility and permeability requirements, often needing a second aggregate or geotextile filter layer; trench size depends on aggregate inflow capacity.
sections.body: The classic drain is an aggregate-filled trench with a pipe near its base (p. 9-105). The drainage aggregate must be filter compatible with the subgrade and permeable enough for flow; a stabilization layer used as a drainage blanket must meet the same requirements. These diametrically opposite requirements often cannot be met by one layer, so a second filter layer (aggregate or geotextile) may be required. Trench size also depends on the inflow capacity of the aggregate: low permeability sand needs a much larger trench perimeter than open graded gravel with a geotextile filter wrap.
sections.applicability: Selecting drain aggregate and filters.

sections.title: Design Overview
sections.summary: Design overview for drainage stabilization: filtration design, dewatering before rubblization, pipe access and drains extending into rock, and the design steps with Darcy, filter, Manning and outlet spacing equations.
sections.body: This section covers design considerations (7.3.1), design steps (7.3.2) and references (7.3.3) for drainage stabilization (pp. 9-105 to 9-109).
sections.applicability: Designing drainage for subgrade stabilization.

sections.title: Design Considerations
sections.summary: Drainage design considerations: engineered graded filters or geotextile filters, draining the subgrade well before rubblization or full depth reclamation, edgedrains also draining the HMA-rubblized PCC interface, upstream pipe access, and underdrains at least 6 in. into rock in rock or shale cuts.
sections.body: Graded granular materials in drains or blankets need proper filtration design; unless flow, piping resistance, clogging resistance and constructability are specified the system may not perform; properly designed geotextile filters can be used instead or with more open graded aggregate (p. 9-105). Dewatering can stabilize a subgrade too weak to support rubblization of concrete or full depth reclamation of asphalt: if the investigation shows the drains can remove moisture, install them well before construction to allow strength gain; the edgedrain should drain the subgrade and remove moisture under the rubblized concrete and at the HMA-rubblized PCC interface, particularly in rolling terrain; inspect and repair existing edgedrains left in place. Include pipe access at the upstream end of drain lines for camera inspection, testing and flushing. In rock or shale cuts, underdrains should extend at least 6 inches into the rock; if too high, water accumulates at the rock-soil interface and destabilizes the subgrade (p. 9-106).
key_points: Install drains well before rubblization where the subgrade is too weak to support it (p. 9-105).
Provide pipe access at the upstream end of drain lines for inspection and flushing.
In rock or shale cuts, extend underdrains at least 6 in. into the rock (p. 9-106).
sections.applicability: Laying out drains for stabilization and rehabilitation projects.

sections.title: Design Steps
sections.summary: Six design steps for drainage stabilization: select drain types, test soils for D85, D60, D15, D10 and permeability, compute flows by Darcy's law (Eq. 9-9) and pavement discharge methods (DRIP), check aggregate filters (Eqs. 9-10 to 9-12), size outlets by Manning (Eqs. 9-13, 9-14, max 250 ft), and draw sections.
sections.body: Step 1: evaluate the need and select alternatives (deep drains and underdrains, edgedrains, interceptor drains, stabilization drainage blanket, capillary barrier, drains for rubblization, or combinations) (p. 9-106). Step 2: on soils adjacent to the drain obtain D85, D60, D15 and D10 and permeability (e.g., ASTM D2434); specify the stabilization layer gradation and estimate its permeability. Step 3: calculate flow and dimension the system, using a collector pipe to reduce drain size. General case: Darcy's law (Eq. 9-9) with flow net gradients (Cedergren 1989); typical gradients are less than 1 for roadway drainage when precipitation is the main source; Figure 9-13 (U.S. Navy 1986) gives typical gradations and permeabilities (p. 9-107). Specific drainage systems: FHWA (1980); flow into trenches, Mansur and Kaufman (1962); horizontal blanket and slope drains, Cedergren (1989). Pavement drainage systems: the discharge rate qd for edgedrains and outlets by the pavement infiltration, permeable base (depth-of-flow) or time-to-drain approach (FHWA 2010); the FHWA DRIP program evaluates permeable base, separator, edgedrain and filtration requirements and drainage path length (p. 9-108). Step 4: aggregate gradation by piping, permeability and uniformity criteria (Eqs. 9-10 to 9-12) or a designed geotextile. Step 5: outlet spacing from pipe capacity by Manning's equation (Eq. 9-13; n = 0.012 smooth, 0.024 corrugated) and L <= Q/qd (Eq. 9-14); maximum outlet spacing should not exceed 250 feet for maintenance; a 4-inch minimum diameter smooth wall pipe at a minimum 1% grade is recommended; check ditch elevations to daylight the blanket (p. 9-109). Step 6: prepare pavement cross sections with drainage features.
key_points: Typical hydraulic gradients for roadway drainage are less than 1 when precipitation is the main source (p. 9-107).
Manning n = 0.012 for smooth pipe and 0.024 for corrugated pipe (p. 9-109).
Maximum outlet spacing 250 ft; minimum 4 in. smooth wall pipe at a minimum 1% grade.
Pavement discharge rate by pavement infiltration, permeable base (depth of flow) or time-to-drain approaches; DRIP program (p. 9-108).
equations: Eq. 9-9: q = k i A; Darcy's law, q = infiltration rate, k = effective soil permeability, i = average hydraulic gradient, A = flow area normal to flow
Eq. 9-10: D15 Aggregate < 5 x D85 Subgrade; piping criterion for drain aggregate
Eq. 9-11: D15 Aggregate > 5 x D15 Subgrade; permeability criterion for drain aggregate
Eq. 9-12: D50 Aggregate > 25 x D50 Subgrade; uniformity criterion for drain aggregate (as printed)
Eq. 9-13: Q = (53.01/n) D^(8/3) S^(1/2); Manning's equation for pipe capacity Q (ft3/day), D pipe diameter (in.), S slope (ft/ft), n roughness coefficient
Eq. 9-14: L <= Q/qd; edgedrain outlet spacing L from pipe capacity Q and pavement discharge rate qd
figures: Figure 9-13: Typical gradations and Darcy permeabilities of several aggregate and graded filter materials.
sections.applicability: Sizing drains, filters and outlet spacing for subgrade and pavement drainage.

sections.title: Primary Design References
sections.summary: Primary design references for drainage stabilization: Cedergren (1989), FHWA (2010), FHWA (1999) pavement subsurface drainage design, Mansur and Kaufman (1962) and USACE (1992) ETL 1110-3-435.
sections.body: References (p. 9-109): Cedergren (1989), Seepage, Drainage, and Flow Nets, third edition; FHWA (2010), Geotechnical Aspects of Pavements; FHWA (1999), Pavement Subsurface Drainage Design (NHI course 131026); Mansur and Kaufman (1962), Dewatering, in Foundation Engineering; USACE (1992), Engineering and Design Drainage Layers for Pavements, ETL 1110-3-435.
sections.applicability: Finding drainage design sources.

sections.title: Overview of Construction Specifications and Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Specifications, quality assurance and monitoring for drainage stabilization systems. Subsections cover: Specification Development; Summary of Quality Assurance; Summary of Instrumentation Monitoring and Construction Control.
sections.body: This section covers specification development (7.4.1), quality assurance (7.4.2) and monitoring and construction control (7.4.3) for drainage systems (pp. 9-110 to 9-111).
sections.applicability: Specifying and checking drains.

sections.title: Specification Development
sections.summary: Drainage specifications cover subgrade, stabilization/drainage blanket and trench/edgedrain components, aggregate placement, compaction, pipe placement and grade with conformance measurements, and a contractor quality assurance plan; no construction traffic over drain lines.
sections.body: Design and quality control consider the subgrade, the subgrade stabilization/drainage blanket and the trench/edgedrain (aggregate, pipe, outlet pipe and headwall) (p. 9-110). Specifications should cover material inputs and outputs, care in aggregate placement, compaction, pipe placement and grade, with conformance measurements. The contractor should provide a quality assurance plan including conformance measurements and care to avoid crushing pipe, prevent contamination of aggregate drainage layers and maintain the system. Construction traffic should not traverse drain lines.
sections.applicability: Writing drainage system specifications.

sections.title: Summary of Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Quality assurance of drains: performance-based acceptance criteria, testing by pouring water upstream and measuring outflow, and video inspection, which has cut edgedrain failure rates from up to 40% to less than 5%.
sections.body: The drainage system should be inspected and tested for proper operation near the end of construction, before final acceptance, against performance-based acceptance criteria; otherwise poor construction may not be found until major damage occurs (p. 9-110). Water can be poured on the drainage layer upstream and outflow measured against the expected rate. Video equipment (e.g., borescopes and mini-cameras) is the most effective post-construction evaluation; several agencies improved from edgedrain failure rates of up to 40% to less than 5% through better quality assurance including video, and several states do not accept drains until video inspection shows no damage.
key_points: Better quality assurance with video cameras reduced edgedrain failure rates from up to 40% to less than 5% (p. 9-110).
sections.applicability: Accepting drainage systems.

sections.title: Summary of Instrumentation Monitoring and Construction Control
sections.summary: Monitoring drains: outflow after installation and precipitation with tilt buckets or flow meters, DCP, FWD and GPR for foundation improvement, and small diameter video cameras to log edgedrains.
sections.body: Outlets should be monitored for outflow after installation and after precipitation events (rainfall, snow melt, ground thaw, dust control watering); tilt buckets or flow meters give continuous measurements (p. 9-110). Improvement in foundation support should be measured using DCP, FWD and/or GPR. Small diameter optical tube video cameras with closed circuit systems are probably the most significant development, logging the inside of edgedrains and exposing construction and inspection weaknesses (p. 9-111).
sections.applicability: Monitoring drain performance.

sections.title: Cost Data
sections.summary: Cost data for drainage stabilization: drain costs: edgedrains and underdrains paid by the linear foot, conventional gravel drain with pipe about $10/linear foot ($7 to $12 bid range), outlets and headwalls paid separately, and select granular materials $4 to $10/yd2 for a 12 in. layer.
sections.body: This section gives the cost components for drains used in subgrade stabilization (p. 9-111).
sections.applicability: Estimating drainage cost.

sections.title: Cost Components
sections.summary: Drain costs: edgedrains and underdrains paid by the linear foot, conventional gravel drain with pipe about $10/linear foot ($7 to $12 bid range), outlets and headwalls paid separately, and select granular materials $4 to $10/yd2 for a 12 in. layer.
sections.body: Edgedrains and underdrains are typically paid by the linear foot including aggregate, conduit, labor and equipment; non-perforated outlet pipes and headwalls are paid separately (p. 9-111). Equipment is common to highway projects, so added mobilization is negligible. A conventional gravel drain with a pipe costs on the order of $10/linear foot installed, with recent bids of $7 to $12/linear foot. Select granular materials range from $4/yd2 to $10/yd2 for a 12-inch layer. See GeoTechTools.
key_points: Conventional gravel drain with pipe about $10/linear foot installed, bids $7 to $12 (p. 9-111).
sections.applicability: Pricing drains for stabilization.

sections.title: Moisture Control: Improved Drainage - Geosynthetics
sections.summary: Geosynthetics in pavement drainage: geotextile separators allowing open graded aggregate, geotextile filters for interceptor drains, underdrains and edgedrains, and prefabricated geocomposite drains replacing drain aggregate.
sections.body: Section 8.0 (pp. 9-112 to 9-128) covers geosynthetics that enhance or directly provide drainage for pavement sections: geotextile filters, vertical geocomposite edgedrains and horizontal geocomposite base drains, with filtration and flow capacity design (Eqs. 9-6 to 9-8c and 9-15 to 9-18, Table 9-10).
sections.applicability: Using geotextile filters and geocomposite drains to control moisture beneath pavements.

sections.title: Feasibility Considerations
sections.summary: Geosynthetics for drainage: separators allowing open graded aggregate, filters for drainage aggregate in interceptor drains, underdrains and edgedrains, and prefabricated geocomposite drains as a substitute for drain aggregate.
sections.body: Geosynthetics can both enhance and directly provide drainage for pavement sections (p. 9-112). As discussed in Section 3, geosynthetic separators allow open graded aggregate that gives improved support and drainage during subgrade stabilization. Geosynthetics can also filter drainage aggregate in trench drains for interceptor drains, underdrains and edgedrains installed during construction, and prefabricated geocomposite drains can replace the aggregate in each type of drain.
sections.applicability: Screening geosynthetic drainage options.

sections.title: Applications
sections.summary: Three applications of geosynthetics in drainage: geotextile filters for edgedrains, underdrains and free draining base (over 40 years of use), vertical geocomposite edgedrains, and horizontal geocomposite base drain layers of stiff geonet composites.
sections.body: There are three applications (p. 9-112): (1) geotextiles as filters for edgedrains, underdrains and free draining base, the most common use, well established with over 40 years of success, having replaced graded granular filters in almost all drainage applications for comparable performance, economy, consistent properties and ease of placement, but requiring proper design; (2) geocomposites placed vertically as edgedrains, whose early growth was stifled by quality and installation problems but which have resurged with improved specifications, ASTM standards and installation guidelines, also used during and after rubblization; (3) geocomposites placed horizontally beneath the base/subbase or pavement as a base drain layer, relatively new: stiff, low compressibility, high flow geonet composites from landfill use, placed below or above a dense graded base, beneath full depth asphalt, as a capillary break or between a crack and seat concrete surface and a new overlay (p. 9-113). Below the base they shorten the drainage path and time-to-drain; directly beneath the surface they intercept infiltration; they are tied into an edgedrain system.
key_points: Geotextile filters have over 40 years of successful use and have replaced graded granular filters in almost all drainage applications (p. 9-112).
A horizontal geocomposite beneath the base shortens the drainage path and reduces time-to-drain (p. 9-113).
sections.applicability: Choosing among geotextile filters, geocomposite edgedrains and horizontal geocomposite drains.

sections.title: Advantages and Potential Disadvantages
sections.summary: Heading for the advantages (9.8.1.2.1) and potential disadvantages (9.8.1.2.2, printed 8.2.1.2) of geosynthetic drainage.
sections.body: Heading for the advantages and potential disadvantages of geosynthetic drainage, 9.8.1.2.1 and 9.8.1.2.2 (printed 8.2.1.2); it has no text of its own. (p. 9-113)
sections.applicability: Weighing geosynthetic against aggregate drainage.

sections.title: Advantages
sections.summary: Geotextiles are usually cheaper than graded granular filters: cheaper aggregate, smaller drains, possibly no collector pipe, faster weather-independent construction, less contamination and spoil, lateral drainage and better performance, more sustainable than gravel, and more reliable drains.
sections.body: In most drainage and filtration applications geotextiles can be justified over graded granular filters for cost: less costly drainage aggregate; smaller drains with the same capacity; possible elimination of collector pipes; much faster construction than graded filters, or than trench aggregate and pipe replaced by geocomposite drains ('geocompsite', as printed); placement not weather dependent; less contamination and segregation of drainage aggregate; less excavation and spoil; prevention of saturation of underlying layers with lateral drainage; better pavement drainage; and cost effectiveness and sustainability over gravel. Geosynthetics often increase drain reliability, a significant cost-benefit when the designer is assured of a properly performing drain. (p. 9-113)
key_points: Smaller drains, possibly no collector pipe (p. 9-113).
Faster, weather-independent placement (p. 9-113).
Often increases drainage system reliability (p. 9-113).
sections.applicability: Weighing geosynthetic against aggregate drainage.

sections.title: Potential Disadvantages
sections.summary: Printed 8.2.1.2. Geosynthetic drains are easier to damage than drain stone, geocomposite edgedrains can be hard to maintain, life-cycle benefits of horizontal geocomposite drains are little demonstrated, and filters clog with precipitates near recycled concrete, rubblizing or crack-and-seat work.
sections.body: Printed with the number 8.2.1.2 under 8.1.2, as printed. Potential disadvantages: relatively easy to damage compared to drain stone, needing more care in construction; geocomposite edgedrains in pavements can be hard to maintain; limited demonstration of life-cycle cost benefits for horizontal geocomposite drains. On projects using recycled concrete, rubblizing or crack-and-seat, geotextiles and granular filters are susceptible to clogging by precipitates. (p. 9-114)
key_points: Easier to damage than drain stone (p. 9-114).
Filters clog with precipitates near recycled or rubblized concrete (p. 9-114).
sections.applicability: Weighing geosynthetic against aggregate drainage.

sections.title: Feasibility Evaluations
sections.summary: Heading for geotechnical, environmental and site feasibility of geosynthetic drainage (9.8.1.3.1 to 9.8.1.3.3).
sections.body: Heading for the feasibility evaluations of geosynthetic drainage, 9.8.1.3.1 to 9.8.1.3.3; it has no text of its own. (p. 9-114)
sections.applicability: Site screening for geosynthetic drains.

sections.title: Geotechnical
sections.summary: The drainage considerations of 9.7.1.3.1 apply; the key is the soils to be drained and their hydraulic characteristics, which set the geosynthetic's filtration properties.
sections.body: The considerations of Section 7.1.3.1 for drainage requirements apply also to geosynthetic drainage. The key components are identifying the soils to be drained and their hydraulic characteristics for the geosynthetic's filtration properties. (p. 9-114)
key_points: Soils to be drained set the filtration properties (p. 9-114).
sections.applicability: Site screening for geosynthetic drains.

sections.title: Environmental Considerations
sections.summary: As for granular drains but easier in wet weather and with less spoil from smaller trenches; groundwater pH and alkaline or acidic conditions are needed to choose durable polymers.
sections.body: The same environmental considerations apply, except that wet weather construction is easier than for granular layers. Smaller trenches carry the same flow, so less spoil, though some still needs disposal. Groundwater pH and alkaline or acidic conditions are needed to evaluate durability and select the most durable polymers. (p. 9-114)
key_points: Groundwater pH needed to select durable polymers (p. 9-114).
sections.applicability: Site screening for geosynthetic drains.

sections.title: Site Conditions
sections.summary: Consider the items of 9.7.1.3.3; local aggregate may be cheaper than geosynthetics; groundwater pH or earlier lime stabilization may exclude polyester geosynthetics.
sections.body: Site evaluation should cover the items in Section 7.1.3.3. Availability of on-site aggregate should be explored, as it may be more cost effective than geosynthetics. Groundwater pH and any previous lime stabilization may exclude geosynthetics made with polyester polymers. (p. 9-114)
key_points: Groundwater pH or prior lime may exclude polyester (p. 9-114).
sections.applicability: Site screening for geosynthetic drains.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.summary: Limitations of geosynthetic drainage: geotextiles and granular filters clog with tufa from RCM and should not be placed between RCM and the drain or wrapped around pipes, though they may go beneath and outside the drain; environmental conditions may limit products.
sections.body: Geotextiles (and granular filters) are susceptible to clogging by tufa precipitate from RCM and should not be indiscriminately used to separate RCM from the drain or wrapped around pipes (pp. 9-114 to 9-115). Environmental conditions (Section 8.1.3.2) may limit the geosynthetics considered. Geotextiles should not be placed between RCM and the drain but could be placed beneath and on the outside of the drain to prevent infiltration of subgrade and subbase.
key_points: Do not place geotextiles between RCM and the drain; they may be placed beneath and outside the drain (p. 9-115).
sections.applicability: Avoiding clogging of geosynthetic drains next to recycled concrete.

sections.title: Construction and Materials
sections.summary: Construction steps for geotextile filters and geocomposite drains, and the geosynthetic materials for filters, edgedrains and horizontal drains. Subsections cover: Construction; Geosynthetics.
sections.body: This section covers construction (8.2.1) and the geosynthetics used (8.2.2) for pavement drainage (pp. 9-115 to 9-120).
sections.applicability: Building geosynthetic drainage systems.

sections.title: Construction
sections.summary: Construction of geotextile-lined drains (intimate soil contact, machine direction along flow, overlaps of 1 ft in roadways and 1 to 2 ft in drains, 1 ft of loose cover, 4 in. pipe bedding, 95% AASHTO T 99, 1 ft top overlap; Figure 9-14) and geocomposite edgedrains (two-sided flow, verticality, sand backfill; Figure 9-15; ASTM D6088) and horizontal drains.
sections.body: The geotextile must be in intimate contact with the soil, with no voids; it lines the edgedrain trench, but the top of the trench beside the permeable base is left open for direct flow to the pipe (p. 9-115). Steps: (1) excavate to a smooth graded surface free of debris and cavities; (2) protect the geotextile from exposure; (3) cut to width with allowances for loose placement and overlaps; (4) replace contaminated material; (5) place with the machine direction along the water flow (parallel to the roadway for pavements), loosely but without wrinkles; (6) overlap a minimum of 1 foot in roadways and 1 to 2 feet in drains, more for high flow and heavy construction, pinned on large base drain sites, upstream over downstream (p. 9-116); (7) cover immediately with at least 1 foot of loose aggregate before compaction (thinner lifts need higher survivability), at least 4 inches of bedding stone below a slotted collector pipe, and compact with vibratory equipment to a minimum 95% of AASHTO T 99 unless structural support is needed (higher effort requires Table 9-7 survivability); (8) overlap the edges at the top by at least 1 foot, then backfill (Figure 9-14). Geocomposite drains have a geotextile filter and a core (waffles, meshes, fluted sheets, nets); edgedrains should allow two-sided flow (p. 9-117). Keep panels vertical and positioned, backfill with open graded aggregate, install outlets promptly with stiff outlet pipes, avoid damage, avoid compacting directly against the panel, overlap the filter at joints and beyond ends, detail the tie-in to collectors. Figure 9-15 (Koerner et al. 1994) places sand backfill between aggregate and geocomposite; see ASTM D6088 (p. 9-118). Horizontal drains are laid with roll width perpendicular to the centerline, subbase end dumped, spread by dozer and compacted with a smooth-drum roller, vibration off on the first lift.
key_points: Overlap geotextiles at least 1 ft in roadways and 1 to 2 ft in drains; upstream over downstream (pp. 9-115 to 9-116).
Cover with at least 1 ft of loose aggregate; at least 4 in. of bedding stone below a collector pipe; compact to 95% AASHTO T 99.
Use only geocomposite edgedrains that allow two-sided flow (p. 9-117).
First lift over a horizontal geocomposite: smooth-drum roller with the vibrator off (p. 9-118).
figures: Figure 9-14: Construction procedure for geotextile-lined underdrains.
Figure 9-15: Recommended installation method for prefabricated geocomposite edgedrains.
sections.applicability: Installing geotextile-lined trench drains and geocomposite edgedrains.

sections.title: Geosynthetics
sections.summary: Heading for drainage geosynthetics: geotextile filters, edgedrains and horizontal geocomposite drains (9.8.2.2.1 to 9.8.2.2.3).
sections.body: Heading for the drainage geosynthetics, 9.8.2.2.1 to 9.8.2.2.3; it has no text of its own. (p. 9-118)
sections.applicability: Specifying geotextile filters and geocomposite drain cores.

sections.title: Geotextile Filters
sections.summary: Geotextile filters are selected on the grain size protected, permeability, clogging resistance and physical properties: permittivity, AOS, survivability and endurance. With RCM or rubblized concrete, never place a geotextile between the recycled material and the drain; wrap only beneath and outside.
sections.body: As for aggregate drains, geotextile filter design and selection rest on the grain size of the soil protected, permeability, clogging resistance and physical properties; key properties are permittivity, opening size (Apparent Opening Size, AOS), and survivability and endurance for construction traffic. Where RCM is used or concrete pavements rubblized ('rubbilized', as printed), geotextiles and granular filters can clog with precipitate and should not be indiscriminately used between permeable base and drain or around pipes (p. 9-119); geotextiles should not go between recycled material and drain but may go beneath and outside the drain to keep out subgrade and subbase. (pp. 9-118 to 9-119)
key_points: Key properties: permittivity, AOS, survivability (p. 9-118).
No geotextile between recycled material and drain (p. 9-119).
sections.applicability: Specifying geotextile filters and geocomposite drain cores.

sections.title: Edgedrains
sections.summary: Edgedrain requirements: filtration and clogging, long-term core strength, flow loss from geotextile intrusion, long-term inflow and outflow; select on seepage (Section 7). Long-term core pressure is limited to the 10,000-hour test value or the quick-test crushing pressure divided by five (FHWA 1993).
sections.body: Geocomposite edgedrain requirements: geotextile filtration/clogging; long-term compressive strength of the core; flow reduction from geotextile intrusion into the core; long-term inflow/outflow capacity. The supplied geotextile must meet the filtration requirements of 8.2.2.1, or system safety is compromised. The in-plane flow capacity is selected against the maximum seepage estimated by the procedure of Section 7. The geocomposite must survive installation and compaction of gravel around it and meet short- and long-term strength; long-term design pressure on the core is limited to the maximum pressure sustained in a test of at least 10,000 hours, or the quick-test crushing pressure divided by a safety factor of five (FHWA 1993). Joining and outlet connection details are product specific; outlet spacing, drain gradient, blockage by small animals and freezing should be considered. (p. 9-119)
key_points: Select flow capacity against seepage estimated per Section 7 (p. 9-119).
Long-term core pressure: 10,000-hour test, or crushing pressure / 5 (p. 9-119).
sections.applicability: Specifying geotextile filters and geocomposite drain cores.

sections.title: Horizontal Geocomposite Drains
sections.summary: Horizontal geocomposite drains must be stiff under cyclic traffic and drain the section within about 2 hours, like a 4 in. open-graded base of at least 1000 ft/day (preferably 2000 to 3000): transmissivity 0.004 to 0.01 ft3/sec, and 6 to 22 ft3/day/ft at a 2% grade.
sections.body: The geocomposite must be stiff enough to carry cyclic traffic without significant deformation and have the flow capacity to drain the section rapidly and prevent base saturation; roadway systems typically require complete drainage within 2 hours. A 4-inch open-graded base layer has conventionally met this (Christopher and McGuffey 1997), with permeability of at least 1000 ft/day and preferably 2000 to 3000 ft/day; for comparison, its transmissivity is 0.004 to 0.01 ft3/sec (units as printed), and at a typical 0.02 (2%) gradient it carries 6 to 22 ft3/day/ft length of road. (p. 9-120)
key_points: Complete drainage typically within 2 hours (p. 9-120).
Benchmark: 4 in. open-graded base, k >= 1000 ft/day (p. 9-120).
6 to 22 ft3/day/ft at a 2% grade (p. 9-120).
sections.applicability: Specifying geotextile filters and geocomposite drain cores.

sections.title: Design Overview
sections.summary: Design overview for geosynthetic drainage: filter design common to all three applications and specific design for vertical and horizontal geocomposites, from FHWA (2008).
sections.body: This section covers design considerations (8.3.1), design steps for geotextile filters and prefabricated geocomposite drains (8.3.2) and references (8.3.3) (pp. 9-120 to 9-126).
sections.applicability: Designing geosynthetic drainage.

sections.title: Design Considerations
sections.summary: Design considerations for geosynthetic drains: filter design common to filters, edgedrains and horizontal drains (FHWA 2008), conservative design for critical projects and severe hydraulics, no selection on cost alone, no skipping of required soil-geotextile tests; FHWA criteria validated by Koerner et al. (1994).
sections.body: The three applications (geotextile filters; vertical geocomposite edgedrains; horizontal geocomposite base drains) need similar geotextile filter design but unique requirements for the composites (p. 9-120). The design steps are from FHWA (2008). The level of design and testing depends on the critical nature of the project and the severity of hydraulic and soil conditions; for critical projects and severe hydraulic conditions very conservative designs are recommended. Geotextile selection should not be based on cost alone, as the geotextile cost is usually minor compared with the drainage system; do not eliminate laboratory soil-geotextile performance testing where the procedure requires it. An NCHRP study (Koerner et al. 1994) found the FHWA criteria an excellent predictor of filter performance, particularly for granular soils (< 50% passing No. 200) (p. 9-121).
key_points: Use very conservative filter designs for critical projects and severe hydraulic conditions (p. 9-120).
Do not select a geotextile on cost alone or skip required soil-geotextile tests.
FHWA criteria predicted filter performance well, especially for soils with < 50% passing No. 200 (p. 9-121).
sections.applicability: Setting the level of design effort for geosynthetic drains.

sections.title: Design Steps
sections.summary: Design steps for geotextile filters and for prefabricated geocomposite drains (edgedrains and horizontal blankets). Subsections cover: Filtration Design for Geotextile Filters; Prefabricated Geocomposite Drain Design.
sections.body: Design steps are given for filtration design of geotextile filters (8.3.2.1) and for prefabricated geocomposite drain design (8.3.2.2) (pp. 9-121 to 9-125).
sections.applicability: Following FHWA design steps for geosynthetic drains.

sections.title: Filtration Design for Geotextile Filters
sections.summary: Geotextile filter design: soil gradation and permeability, retention (Eqs. 9-6, 9-7), permeability and permittivity (Eq. 9-8 and 9-8a to 9-8c: 0.1, 0.2 and 0.5 sec-1 by fines), clogging AOS >= 3 D15 for Cu > 3 (Eq. 9-15), porosity and open area qualifiers, and Table 9-10 survivability classes.
sections.body: Step 1: determine the gradation of the soil directly adjacent to the drain: D85, D15 and percent finer than No. 200 (p. 9-121). Step 2: determine its permeability. Step 3: apply the AOS, permeability and permittivity criteria (Eqs. 9-6 to 9-8, after FHWA 2008); for noncohesive silts and highly pumping soils use AOS <= D85 and run filtration tests. Filter permittivity (ASTM D4491) is greater than for separation and rises with fines: psi >= 0.1 sec-1 for > 50% passing No. 200 (Eq. 9-8a), >= 0.2 for 15 to 50% (Eq. 9-8b), >= 0.5 for < 15% (Eq. 9-8c) (pp. 9-121 to 9-122). Clogging: for steady flow, low gradient and well graded or uniform upstream soil, AOS >= 3 x D15 (Eq. 9-15) for soils with Cu > 3; for Cu ≤ 3 use the maximum AOS from retention; nonwoven porosity ≥ 50%; woven percent open area ≥ 4%; or run filtration tests for critical and severe applications. Step 4: survivability per AASHTO M 288 (Table 9-10, p. 9-123): grab strength 315 / 200 lb (Class 1, < 50% / ≥ 50% elongation) and 250 / 157 lb (Class 2); seam 260 / 180 and 220 / 140 lb; tear 110 / 80 and 90 / 56 lb; puncture 620 / 433 and 495 / 309 lb; UV 50% after 500 hours. Use Class 2 for edgedrain filters and separation layers with subgrade CBR > 3 and normal equipment (keeping at least 6 inches of base/subbase between wheel and geotextile); use Class 1 for filters in drainage blankets and capillary barriers with CBR < 3 and heavy equipment.
key_points: Clogging: AOS >= 3 x D15 of upstream soil for Cu > 3; nonwoven porosity ≥ 50%; woven open area ≥ 4%.
Table 9-10: Class 1 grab strength 315 lb (< 50% elongation) or 200 lb (≥ 50%); Class 2 250 lb or 157 lb (p. 9-123).
Class 1 for drainage blankets and capillary barriers over CBR < 3 with heavy equipment.
equations: Eq. 9-6: AOS <= D85 subgrade (Wovens); geotextile retention criterion
Eq. 9-7: AOS <= 1.8 x D85 subgrade (Nonwovens); geotextile retention criterion
Eq. 9-8: k Geotextile > k Soil and psi >= 0.1 sec^-1; geotextile permeability and permittivity criterion
Eq. 9-8a: psi >= 0.1 sec^-1; filter permittivity for > 50% passing No. 200 (0.075 mm)
Eq. 9-8b: psi >= 0.2 sec^-1; filter permittivity for 15 to 50% passing No. 200
Eq. 9-8c: psi >= 0.5 sec^-1; filter permittivity for < 15% passing No. 200
Eq. 9-15: AOS >= 3 x D15 Upstream Soil; clogging criterion for steady flow, low gradient, soils with Cu > 3

sections.title: Prefabricated Geocomposite Drain Design
sections.summary: Three-step design of prefabricated geocomposite edgedrains (PGED) and horizontal geocomposite blankets: filtration per 8.3.2.1, flow capacity from transmissivity by Darcy's law (Eqs. 9-16, 9-17; ASTM D4716) and edgedrain capacity Q = C D (S + (D1 - D2)/L)^(1/2) (Eq. 9-18; C typically 0.5 to 2.5).
sections.body: Three basic steps apply to a PGED or a horizontal geocomposite drainage blanket (p. 9-123). Step 1: design for filtration without clogging or piping per Section 8.3.2.1 (AOS, k, psi). Step 2: design for adequate inflow/outflow capacity under design loads for the maximum anticipated seepage over the design life: estimate qd per Section 7.3.2 Step 3 (for a horizontal blanket the inflow gradient is vertical, i = 1, and outflow uses the drain slope, i = SL), then select the geocomposite; flow capacity comes from transmissivity measured by ASTM D4716; the maximum flow per unit width of a horizontal drain follows Darcy's law (Eqs. 9-16 and 9-17) (p. 9-124). The capacity of a vertical geocomposite edgedrain is Eq. 9-18, with C the manufacturer-supplied PGED flow factor in ft3/day/inch (typical range 0.5 to 2.5), D the averaged depth of flow (D1 + D2)/2 in inches, D1 depth of flow zone and D2 depth of outlet (outlet pipe diameter) in ft, S longitudinal slope and L outlet spacing in ft (p. 9-125); Figure 9-16 (FHWA 1998) shows the inputs. The text introduces the steps as three; the third is not separately printed in this passage.
key_points: For a horizontal blanket, inflow gradient i = 1 and outflow gradient i = SL (p. 9-124).
Transmissivity is measured by ASTM D4716.
PGED flow factor C typically ranges from 0.5 to 2.5 ft3/day/inch (p. 9-125).
equations: Eq. 9-16: q = kp i A = kp i B t; flow capacity of a geosynthetic by Darcy's law, kp = in-plane permeability, B = width, t = thickness, i = gradient
Eq. 9-17: q/B = theta i; flow per unit width from transmissivity theta (= kp t)
Eq. 9-18: Q = C D (S + (D1 - D2)/L)^(1/2); geocomposite edgedrain capacity Q (ft3/day/ft), C = PGED flow factor, D = averaged depth of flow, S = longitudinal slope, L = outlet spacing
figures: Figure 9-16: Schematic diagrams for computing flow of PGED: a roadway cross section (top) and an edgedain cross section (bottom).

sections.body: This section covers specification development (8.4.1), quality assurance (8.4.2) and monitoring and construction control (8.4.3) for geosynthetic drainage (pp. 9-126 to 9-127).

sections.title: Specification Development
sections.summary: Specifications for geosynthetic drainage: AASHTO M 288 guide geotextile specifications for drainage and trench drains, properties chosen by project criticality, hydraulic severity, soil and installation, and ASTM D7001 for edgedrain geocomposites.
sections.body: AASHTO M 288 (2014a) includes guide geotextile specifications for routine drainage and filtration and trench drains (p. 9-126). Hydraulic and physical properties must be selected for the nature of the project (critical or less critical), hydraulic conditions (severe or less severe), soil conditions and appropriate construction and installation procedures. ASTM D7001 is the standard specification for Geocomposites for Pavement Edgedrains and Other High-Flow Applications.
sections.applicability: Writing specifications for geosynthetic drains.

sections.title: Summary of Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Installation checklist for geotextile-lined trench drains: smooth trench, no soil falling in, full contact without wrinkles, compacted bedding (typically 3/4 in. gravel), exhuming about 1 ft2 to check damage, choked and compacted stone around the pipe, and a top overlap of at least 1 ft.
sections.body: Attention goes to aggregate placement, geotextile damage and overlaps at the trench top and roll ends (p. 9-126). Checklist: (1) trench without large voids or sharp protrusions; (2) observe roll-out, keeping excavated or loose soil out of the trench and off the geotextile; (3) no wrinkles or folds and full contact on bottom, sides and corners (p. 9-127); (4) initial aggregate (typically 3/4-inch gravel) placed and compacted as a pipe bedding layer to the drawing thickness; (5) in one small section remove about 1 square foot of stone to check for damage, and if damaged reduce the drop height; (6) stone choked under the pipe edges and compacted per specification; (7) geotextile folded over the gravel with an overlap of at least 1 foot or the trench width if smaller; (8) overlap maintained while placing cover soil or asphalt.
key_points: Remove about 1 ft2 of stone in one section to check for damage; reduce drop height if damaged (p. 9-127).
Top overlap at least 1 ft, or the trench width if smaller.
sections.applicability: Inspecting geotextile-lined trench drain installation.

sections.title: Summary of Instrumentation Monitoring and Construction Control
sections.summary: Monitoring geosynthetic drains: outflow after installation and precipitation with tilt buckets or flow meters, DCP, FWD and GPR for support improvement, and video inspection of all outlets and drain lines on all projects.
sections.body: Drain outlets should be monitored for outflow after installation and after precipitation events (rainfall, snow melt, ground thaw, dust control watering), using tilt buckets or flow meters for continuous records (p. 9-127). Improvement in foundation support should be measured by DCP, FWD and/or GPR. Video inspection of all outlets and drain lines should be required on all projects.
key_points: Video inspection of all outlets and drain lines should be required on all projects (p. 9-127).
sections.applicability: Monitoring geosynthetic drains.

Geocomposite pavement edgedrains typically cost $1.00 to $3.00/linear foot installed, while a conventional geotextile wrapped gravel drain with a pipe is on the order of $9.00/linear foot installed. sections.title: Moisture Control: Partial and Full Encapsulation
sections.summary: Moisture control of expansive subgrades by partial encapsulation along the pavement edge or full encapsulation with geomembranes, which delays rather than eliminates expansive soil problems.
sections.body: Section 9.0 (pp. 9-129 to 9-137) covers geomembrane encapsulation of expansive subgrade soils to limit moisture change and the resulting swell and shrink: feasibility, construction and materials, design methods for barrier depth, specifications and quality assurance, and cost.
sections.applicability: Controlling moisture change in expansive pavement subgrades.

sections.title: Feasibility Considerations
sections.summary: Feasibility considerations for partial and full encapsulation of expansive soils. Subsections cover: Applications; Advantages and Potential Disadvantages; Feasibility Evaluations; Limitations.
sections.body: This section covers applications, advantages and disadvantages, feasibility evaluations and limitations of encapsulation (pp. 9-129 to 9-131).
sections.applicability: Screening encapsulation for expansive soils.

sections.title: Applications
sections.summary: Encapsulation applications: partial encapsulation along the pavement edge (Figure 9-17) or full encapsulation (Figure 9-18) of expansive soils where moisture fluctuates; geomembranes horizontal, vertical or both; delays but does not eliminate the problem, the permanent fix being removal and replacement.
sections.body: Where expansive soils occur with significant expected subgrade moisture fluctuation, partial encapsulation along the pavement edge (Figure 9-17) or full encapsulation (Figure 9-18) reduces moisture change and retards swelling and/or shrinkage (p. 9-129). Full encapsulation completely surrounds the soil with geomembranes to prevent moisture entering or leaving; partial encapsulation minimizes water entering or leaving through the pavement surface, joints, cracks and edges. The geomembrane moisture barrier is placed horizontally, vertically or both, minimizing pavement distress, cracking and slab distortion. The method delays potential problems and does not completely eliminate them; the only permanent solution is to remove and replace the expansive soil with sufficient overburden to resist the swell potential, which is not always feasible (p. 9-130).
key_points: Encapsulation delays expansive soil problems; the only permanent solution is removal and replacement with sufficient overburden (p. 9-130).
sections.applicability: Pavements on expansive soils subject to seasonal moisture change.

sections.title: Advantages and Potential Disadvantages
sections.summary: Heading for the advantages (9.9.1.2.1, printed 9.2.1.1) and potential disadvantages (9.9.1.2.2) of encapsulation.
sections.body: Heading for the advantages and potential disadvantages of encapsulation, 9.9.1.2.1 (printed 9.2.1.1) and 9.9.1.2.2; it has no text of its own. (p. 9-130)

sections.title: Advantages
sections.summary: Printed 9.2.1.1. Encapsulation is relatively fast and easy to place, prevents or minimizes damage from long-term moisture changes, suits rapid renewal, and gives long-lived facilities.
sections.body: Printed with the number 9.2.1.1 under 9.1.2, as printed. Advantages: relatively fast and easy placement; prevents or minimizes damage from long-term moisture changes; suitable for rapid renewal of transportation facilities; and provides long-lived facilities. (p. 9-130)

sections.title: Potential Disadvantages
sections.summary: Encapsulation lacks simple, reliable, non-proprietary analysis and design procedures, established parameters and long-term performance criteria, and easy selection tools.
sections.body: Potential disadvantages: lack of simple, comprehensive, reliable and non-proprietary analysis and design procedures; lack of established engineering parameters and/or performance criteria, especially for long-term performance; and lack of easy-to-use tools for technology selection. (p. 9-130)

sections.summary: Heading for geotechnical, environmental and site feasibility of encapsulation (9.9.1.3.1 to 9.9.1.3.3).
sections.body: Heading for the feasibility evaluations of encapsulation, 9.9.1.3.1 to 9.9.1.3.3; it has no text of its own. (p. 9-130)

sections.title: Geotechnical
sections.summary: Expansive soils shrink and swell with seasonal moisture, cracking pavement edges and roughening the surface. The key is the depth to encapsulate (set by moisture below the barrier, affinity for water, swell pressure and needed overburden) or, for partial encapsulation, the barrier depth from allowable moisture change, membrane diffusion and the active zone.
sections.body: Expansive soils change volume with seasonal moisture, by an amount depending on shrink-swell potential and moisture change; drying shrinks and wetting swells them, causing longitudinal cracks near the pavement edge and significant roughness along its length. The key issue is the depth of soil to encapsulate, or the barrier penetration depth for partial encapsulation. Full encapsulation depth depends on the moisture content below the barrier, its affinity for more moisture, the swell pressure and the overburden needed to prevent further swell. Partial encapsulation depth depends on the allowable moisture change in the encapsulated soil over a specified time, against the membrane's diffusion coefficient and the active zone of moisture activity (p. 9-131). (pp. 9-130 to 9-131)
key_points: Expansive soils crack pavement edges and roughen the surface (p. 9-130).
Full encapsulation depth set by swell pressure and needed overburden (p. 9-130).
Partial: barrier depth from allowable moisture change and active zone (p. 9-131).
sections.applicability: Investigating a site for encapsulation.

sections.title: Environmental Considerations
sections.summary: Temperature, its variation, humidity, rain and wind matter: liners need special care in cold weather and are not installed in rain; some barriers are temperature sensitive, moisture and wind affect field seaming, and field impregnated coated geotextiles need defined weather.
sections.body: Temperature and its variation, humidity, rainfall and wind must be considered. Geosynthetic liners need special selection and installation for cold weather and should not be installed during rain; some barriers are more temperature sensitive than others, and moisture and wind affect field seaming. Barriers of field impregnated coated geotextiles must be placed in carefully defined weather. (p. 9-131)
key_points: Do not install liners in rain (p. 9-131).
sections.applicability: Investigating a site for encapsulation.

sections.title: Site Conditions
sections.summary: Determine soil type, moisture, plasticity, expansive layer thickness and depth, subgrade stiffness, long-term and perched water and seepage (for interceptor drains), and rocky layers that set liner protection.
sections.body: Site conditions include soil type, in situ moisture and plasticity, and thickness and depth of expansive layers; subgrade stiffness to judge whether more improvement is needed; long-term groundwater and perched water levels and seepage directions, to evaluate interceptor drains limiting water access; and rocky layers, which set protection at the base of excavations and for fill over the liner. (p. 9-131)
key_points: Locate groundwater, perched water and seepage for interceptor drains (p. 9-131).
Rocky layers set liner protection (p. 9-131).
sections.applicability: Investigating a site for encapsulation.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.summary: Limitations of geomembrane encapsulation of expansive subgrades: liners may not be placeable in inclement weather, and partial encapsulation needs long-term maintenance to be considered in selection.
sections.body: It may not be feasible to place liners in inclement weather, and partial encapsulation must consider long-term maintenance in the selection of this technology (p. 9-131).
sections.applicability: Recognizing limits on encapsulation.

sections.title: Construction and Materials
sections.summary: Construction and materials for geomembrane encapsulation of expansive subgrades: encapsulation construction: full encapsulation by excavation, bitumen spray at about 1 gal/yd2, geomembrane or bitumen-coated geotextile, backfill in lifts and fold-over seams; partial encapsulation by edge trenches 2.5 to 4 in. wide and 5 to 10 ft deep with the membrane on the shoulder side and flowable fill backfill.
sections.body: This section covers construction (9.2.1) and materials (9.2.2) for encapsulation (pp. 9-131 to 9-133).
sections.applicability: Building encapsulated subgrades.

sections.title: Construction
sections.summary: Encapsulation construction: full encapsulation by excavation, bitumen spray at about 1 gal/yd2, geomembrane or bitumen-coated geotextile, backfill in lifts and fold-over seams; partial encapsulation by edge trenches 2.5 to 4 in. wide and 5 to 10 ft deep with the membrane on the shoulder side and flowable fill backfill.
sections.body: The subgrade, its preparation, panel deployment, the overlying fill type and its placement and compaction all affect barrier survivability (p. 9-131). Full encapsulation: excavate the entire soil mass to depth; prepare a level surface; spray the base with bitumen at approximately 1 gal/yd2 (slippage resistance, puncture protection, extra seal); place the geomembrane, or a geotextile to be coated with bitumen, on the base and up and over the side slopes far enough to encapsulate the surface; apply bitumen to a geotextile liner; backfill and compact in lifts; fold over the liner, overlapping and sealing seams; place a roadbed layer over the liner (p. 9-132). Partial encapsulation: excavate a trench on both sides of the roadway, 2.5 to 4 inches wide and 5 to 10 feet deep; lay the geomembrane in the trench on the shoulder side, using a dispenser that passes it around a bar at 45 degrees; place the coated side of coated geotextiles against the trench wall; use a tougher, thicker geomembrane where construction damage is expected; seam overlaps (welding or sprayed bitumen); backfill with flowable fill (medium-graded sand, a small percentage of cement, a large portion of fly ash and water); extend the membranes over the subgrade, ideally across the whole surface, and seam at the centerline.
key_points: Spray the excavation base with bitumen at approximately 1 gal/yd2 for full encapsulation (p. 9-132).
Partial encapsulation trenches are 2.5 to 4 in. wide and 5 to 10 ft deep, membrane on the shoulder side.
Backfill partial encapsulation trenches with flowable fill so the geomembrane is not damaged.
sections.applicability: Field construction of full and partial encapsulation.

sections.title: Materials
sections.summary: Encapsulation materials: CSPE, EIA, EPDM, HDPE, LLDPE, PP or PVC geomembranes in rolls 650 to 1,000 ft long and 15 to 35 ft wide, typically 40 mils, with nonwoven cushions (typically 8 oz/yd2 over rocky soil), roughened sheets against slippage, and field-coated nonwovens of 6 to 12 oz/yd2.
sections.body: Most standard geomembranes can be used: CSPE, EIA, EPDM, HDPE, LLDPE, PP, PVC and others, supplied in rolls 650 to 1,000 feet long and approximately 15 to 35 feet wide or in panels; order widths that fit the design to minimize field cutting and seaming (p. 9-133). Typical membrane thickness for encapsulation is 40 mils. A nonwoven geotextile cushion above the liner protects it during fill placement; a roughened geomembrane should be considered to avoid slippage of the geotextile and roadbed. For full encapsulation over rocky soils a geotextile cushion is also needed beneath the liner. Liners can be built in place from nonwoven geotextiles field coated with asphalt, rubber-bitumen, emulsified asphalt or polymer formulations (possibly proprietary), commonly 6 to 12 oz/yd2; sprayed-on membranes are seam-free but bubbles and pinholes can form, so the geotextile must be clean and dry. For rocky subgrades, 8 oz/yd2 needle punched nonwovens are typically used as the protection layer.
key_points: Typical encapsulation geomembrane thickness is 40 mils (p. 9-133).
Rolls 650 to 1,000 ft long and about 15 to 35 ft wide.
Protection layer over rocky subgrade: typically 8 oz/yd2 needle punched nonwoven.
sections.applicability: Selecting geomembranes and cushions for encapsulation.

sections.title: Design Overview
sections.summary: Design overview for encapsulation: barrier depth by climate-based (Picornell-Darder 1985) or diffusion-based (Lord and Koerner 1986) methods. Subsections cover: Design Considerations; Design Steps; Primary Design References.
sections.body: This section covers design considerations (9.3.1), design steps (9.3.2) and references (9.3.3) for encapsulation (pp. 9-134 to 9-135).
sections.applicability: Designing encapsulation.

sections.title: Design Considerations
sections.summary: Encapsulation design is mainly empirical and rational; the main issue is the minimum installation depth, by the climatic moisture barrier method (Picornell-Darder 1985) or membrane diffusion method (Lord and Koerner 1986), plus a depth whose overburden prevents heave from swell pressure tests.
sections.body: Current geomembrane design methods are based primarily on empirical evidence and rational principles; the main issue is the minimum depth of installation (p. 9-134). Two methods are available: the depth of a vertical moisture barrier from climatic conditions (Picornell-Darder 1985), and water diffusion through the membrane from the diffusion coefficient of the soil (Lord and Koerner 1986). Another consideration is a depth giving a stable condition (no moisture change) such that the overburden of the encapsulated material prevents heave, based on swell pressure tests.
sections.applicability: Setting the depth of an encapsulation barrier.

sections.title: Design Steps
sections.summary: Encapsulation design steps: depth of the base or vertical barrier, typically 5 to 10 ft (Steinberg 1998), by Picornell-Darder's drought-frequency and suction method or Lord and Koerner's diffusion method; then constant resilient modulus over pavement life, with caution on the EICM for partial encapsulation.
sections.body: Step 1: determine the depth to the base of the encapsulation layer or the vertical depth of the partial encapsulation geomembrane, typically 5 to 10 feet (Steinberg 1998) (p. 9-134). Method 1 (Picornell-Darder 1985): gather climate and soil information; select the design event from a frequency analysis of drought intensities over a stochastic series of one-year events; estimate soil deformation either by numerical simulation of water flow or, neglecting flux, from the suction profile for the minimum stored water in the design year; extend the barrier through the zone of seasonal moisture change. Method 2 (Lord and Koerner 1986): from the soil diffusion coefficient and a half-space model, obtain the water content change of the encapsulated mass over time as a function of membrane diffusion coefficient; select an allowable moisture change for a specified time; determine membrane thickness and diffusion coefficient (p. 9-135). Step 2: with constant moisture over time, the resilient modulus can be assumed constant over the pavement life; with partial encapsulation, use of the Enhanced Integrated Climatic Model (EICM) in M-E design to predict moisture change calls for caution.
key_points: Encapsulation or vertical barrier depth is typically 5 to 10 ft (Steinberg 1998) (p. 9-134).
With moisture held constant, resilient modulus can be assumed constant over the pavement life (p. 9-135).
Use caution with the EICM moisture prediction for partial encapsulation.
sections.applicability: Sizing encapsulation depth and assigning subgrade modulus.

sections.title: Primary Design References
sections.summary: Primary design references for encapsulation of expansive subgrades: FHWA (2010), Lord and Koerner (1986) diffusion method, Picornell-Darder (1985) moisture barrier depth and Steinberg (1998).
sections.body: References (p. 9-135): FHWA (2010), Geotechnical Aspects of Pavements; Lord and Koerner (1986), Diffusion of Water from Soils Encapsulated by Impregnated Geotextiles (MESLs); Picornell-Darder (1985), design criteria to select the depth of a vertical moisture barrier; Steinberg (1998), Geomembranes and the Control of Expansive Soils in Construction.

sections.title: Geosynthetics – Overview of Construction Specifications and Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Specifications, quality assurance and monitoring for geomembrane encapsulation. Subsections cover: Specification Development; Summary of Quality Assurance; Summary of Instrumentation Monitoring and Construction Control.
sections.body: This section covers specification development (9.4.1), quality assurance (9.4.2) and monitoring and construction control (9.4.3) for encapsulation (pp. 9-135 to 9-137).
sections.applicability: Specifying and checking encapsulation.

sections.title: Specification Development
sections.summary: Specifications for partial encapsulation: method or, typically, performance approach; contractor submittals of geomembrane details and a quality assurance plan; FHWA (2008) guidelines; complete, not overly elaborate specifications; installers certified by the International Association of Geosynthetic Installers.
sections.body: Method approach or performance approach specifications may be used (p. 9-135). Method specifications state a specific pattern, procedure and equipment and should be used only if the agency understands partial encapsulation well; performance specifications are therefore typically used, giving the contractor flexibility and most of the risk (p. 9-136). Either way the contractor submits geomembrane details (manufacturer, product, composition, strength) and the owner checks materials and work. FHWA (2008) gives guide geomembrane specifications with commentary. The specification should be complete enough to bid without more information, not require overly elaborate or expensive methods, contain the quality assurance requirements, require a detailed contractor quality assurance plan for liner installation, and set minimum contractor qualifications and a preconstruction meeting. The installer should be certified by the International Association of Geosynthetic Installers.
key_points: Performance approach specifications are typically used for partial encapsulation (p. 9-136).
The geomembrane installer should be certified by the International Association of Geosynthetic Installers.
sections.applicability: Writing encapsulation specifications.

sections.title: Summary of Quality Assurance
sections.summary: Quality assurance of encapsulation: crucial installation control, moisture variation of the encapsulated layer over the design life, optimum moisture and maximum dry density checked by sand cone or nuclear gauge, field CBR or LFWD at mid-depth and surface, and post-construction elevation monitoring.
sections.body: Quality control during geomembrane installation is crucial (p. 9-136). Quality assurance includes determining the moisture variation of the encapsulated layer at different times from construction to the end of the design life. During construction, optimum moisture content and maximum dry density are determined by ASTM or AASHTO standards and monitored by sand cone and/or nuclear gauge. Field CBR or LFWD tests at mid-depth of the fill and at the surface can establish design parameters. Pavement performance, including surface elevation changes related to moisture changes, should be monitored after construction.
sections.applicability: Field quality checks on encapsulation.

sections.title: Summary of Instrumentation Monitoring and Construction Control
sections.summary: Monitoring encapsulation: GPR and TDR (ASTM D6565) for moisture, level surveys or Benkelman beam for shrink and swell, strain gages on the liner, and periodic FWD tests.
sections.body: Moisture variation of the encapsulated layer can be monitored with GPR and Time Domain Reflectometry (TDR, ASTM D6565) (p. 9-136). Future shrinkage or swell can be measured on the roadway surface by level surveys or the Benkelman beam test. Strain gages on the liner can indicate movement from moisture changes. FWD tests can be run periodically to monitor pavement performance and subgrade support (p. 9-137).
sections.applicability: Monitoring encapsulated subgrades.

sections.title: Geosynthetic Cost Data
sections.summary: Cost data for geomembrane encapsulation: encapsulation costs: geomembrane by the square yard in place at about $2.50 to $10/yd2 (2009-2010 bids, bitumen coated geotextiles in the lower half), excavation and replacement including flowable fill by the cubic yard, higher unit costs for specialized applications, and negligible mobilization.
sections.body: This section gives the cost components for encapsulation (p. 9-137).
sections.applicability: Estimating encapsulation cost.

sections.title: Cost Components
sections.summary: Encapsulation costs: geomembrane by the square yard in place at about $2.50 to $10/yd2 (2009-2010 bids, bitumen coated geotextiles in the lower half), excavation and replacement including flowable fill by the cubic yard, higher unit costs for specialized applications, and negligible mobilization.
sections.body: The primary pay items beyond normal subgrade work are the geomembrane by the square yard in place and excavation and replacement, including flowable fill if required, by the cubic yard (p. 9-137). Installed geomembrane prices from 2009 and 2010 bids were on the order of $2.50 to $10/yd2, with bitumen coated geotextiles generally in the lower half; membrane specifications (weight, strength) strongly influence cost. Specialized applications such as bridge approaches and isolated embankments cost more per unit than mass applications such as a complete roadway section. Equipment is common to highway work, so mobilization is negligible; production rates are controlled by related activities (base placement, paving), and resources adjust with little effect on total cost.
key_points: Installed geomembrane about $2.50 to $10/yd2 (2009-2010 bids), bitumen coated geotextiles in the lower half (p. 9-137).
